detail.title: A Multiscale Optimization Framework for Real-World Transportation and Network Design Problems
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of global supply chains and the increasing availability of data have madelogistics optimization a critical yet increasingly complex challenge for industries worldwide. Solving transportation and network design problems is essential for optimizing supply chains, yet the complexity of real-world instances often renders direct optimization infeasible. In addressing this challenge, various aggregation schemes have been proposed, attempting to exploit hidden global structure and redundancies in the input data. While practically successful, these methods do no allow for interactivity in the optimization or interpretation of a solution, and have been applied to models with linear or convex cost structures. We propose a novel framework that dynamically aggregates and refines network data, tariffs, and demands, enabling the efficient transfer of feasible solutions across scales. In contrast to traditional approaches we employ a dynamic data structure enabling independent modification of the level of detail in different parts of the network. We customize our framework to a multi-commodity flow model with piecewise linear costs and a facility location model with delivery time constraints, incorporating diverse industry-specific aspects validated by experienced logistics professionals. The method is evaluated on real-world data from the automotive industry, provided by the supply chain consulting company 4flow. Results demonstrate significantly improved solution quality and, beyond computational performance,highlight the practical value of the approach through its support for explainability and interactivity: decision-makers can navigate between different levels of aggregation to better understand, validate, and communicate optimization outcomes, facilitating adoption in real-world supply chain planning.

title: Specialisation as a Relational Condition: A Derivation of Firms and Markets
affiliations: InterAgency Institute

detail.title: Specialisation as a Relational Condition: A Derivation of Firms and Markets
detail.abstract: This paper develops an account of specialisation in which economic behaviour is understood as the evolved set of processes through which agents act on the probability of resource-services being available when and where wanted. Specialisation is treated as a relational condition in which an agent's range of direct productive activity is narrower than the range of their wants, sustained by relations with other agents whose activity is similarly concentrated on different ranges. The paper derives the structural requirements that deepening specialisation places on its two sides: firm-like organisation as the form through which sustained concentrated production is carried, and market institutions as the form through which distributional conversion at scale is supported. Firms and markets, on this account, are co-evolved elaborations of specialisation's two sides rather than parallel alternatives or sequentially prior arrangements. The paper engages with the classical, neoclassical, growth-theoretic, evolutionary, and transaction-cost traditions, and grounds its account in the trajectory of organisational and institutional forms documented in the anthropological, archaeological, and economic-history literatures.

title: AI Augmented Shipping Automation in ERP Systems:,Architecture, Algorithms, and Production Evaluation

detail.title: AI Augmented Shipping Automation in ERP Systems:,Architecture, Algorithms, and Production Evaluation

keywords.keywords: ERP shipping automation · Oracle EBS · carrier API integration · deep Q-network · reinforcement learning · BERT · LSTM · temporal fusion transformer · retrieval-augmented generation · anomaly detection · CUPS · ZPL · label generation

detail.abstract: Shipping label generation sits at the operational heart of order fulfilment in warehouse environments, yet in many Oracle ERP deployments it still depends on warehouse staff manually re-entering shipment data into carrier portals—a practice that is slow, error-prone, and increasingly incompatible with the throughput demands of modern e-commerce. This paper describes ShipSync-AI, an architecture we developed and deployed in a production Oracle E-Business Suite environment to eliminate that manual step and, beyond it, to embed genuine intelligence into the shipping decision process. The system has two layers. The first is a seven-component integration pipeline that automates end-to-end label generation through direct carrier API communication, with formal treatment of idempotent reprint handling, hierarchical printer resolution, return label support, and exponential-backoff error recovery. The second is an AI Intelligence Layer comprising six modules—a fine-tuned BERT address validator, an LSTM + gradient-boosted ETA predictor, a Deep Q-Network carrier selection agent, an Isolation Forest anomaly detector, a retrieval-augmented LLM exception handler, and a Temporal Fusion Transformer demand forecaster—each formally specified and individually benchmarked. The complete system was evaluated across 187,432 production shipments over 90 days. Manual processing effort fell by 82%, label accuracy reached 99.7%, throughput increased from 45 to 380 labels per hour, and P99 end-to-end latency measured 2.8 seconds. We also document the practical engineering challenges—ZPL resolution mismatches, API versioning transitions, concurrent staging table contention—that sit between a well-specified architecture and a working production deployment.

title: Quantum-inspired bi-level optimization for renewable-integrated vehicle-to-everything energy management in smart grids under uncertainty
affiliations: HUTECH University, Le Quy Don Technical University and HUTECH University

detail.title: Quantum-inspired bi-level optimization for renewable-integrated vehicle-to-everything energy management in smart grids under uncertainty
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a quantum-inspired bi-level optimization framework for renewable-integrated vehicle-to-everything (V2X) energy management in smart grids under uncertainty. The proposed framework simultaneously coordinates renewable generation, electric vehicle (EV) charging/discharging scheduling, vehicle-to-home (V2H), vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), vehicle-to-grid (V2G) energy exchange, operational risk, and user satisfaction. A bi-level optimization model is developed in which the upper level minimizes load variance, electricity procurement cost, carbon emissions, and operational risk. In contrast, the lower level maximizes EV user profit and satisfaction. To solve the resulting nonlinear and stochastic optimization problem, a Quantum-inspired Energy Valley Optimizer (Q-EVO) is developed to improve convergence stability and exploration capability. Monte Carlo sampling is employed to model renewable generation and EV behavioral uncertainties. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework reduces load variance from 12,559.59 kW² to 8,705.60 kW² (30.69%), decreases system operating cost by 14.84%, reduces carbon emissions by 11.18%, and lowers peak net load by 19.96%. In addition, EV user satisfaction consistently remains above 0.99633 under all stochastic scenarios, confirming strong robustness and reliable user-level performance. Comparative results further demonstrate that the proposed Q-EVO provides superior optimization performance and convergence behavior compared with benchmark metaheuristic algorithms.

title: Pricing Sustainability or Pricing Illiquidity? Evidence from ESG Index Futures
affiliations: University of Glasgow, Glasgow University, Inland Norway University of Applied Sciences and Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

detail.title: Pricing Sustainability or Pricing Illiquidity? Evidence from ESG Index Futures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None of the authors has anything to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received.

detail.abstract: We investigate whether ESG index futures embed a distinct sustainability-related risk premium or whether pricing differences relative to conventional futures mainly reflect market frictions, especially lower relative liquidity. Using daily data on S&P 500 ESG and standard E-mini futures from 2020-2025 across front-, three-month, and six-month maturities, we construct ESG-conventional forward-premium differentials in unscaled, percentage, and log terms. We relate these differentials to relative open interest, relative spot-index valuation, macro-financial controls, liquidity-state interactions, term-structure specifications, and event-time policy shocks. The results show that the ESG-conventional spread is largely explained by relative liquidity and valuation effects rather than by a persistent sustainability premium. Greater ESG market depth compresses the premium gap, while macro-financial controls play a secondary and state-dependent role. Sensitivity increases with maturity and is strongest when liquidity is scarce, consistent with limits-to-arbitrage mechanisms and weaker arbitrage capacity in thinner ESG futures markets. Event-time regressions and local projections indicate that ESG-related policy shocks generate heterogeneous but short-lived adjustments and explain little medium-run variation once continuous liquidity and valuation channels are accounted for. Overall, ESG futures pricing appears to reflect market microstructure, participation constraints, and relative valuation dynamics rather than a separate sustainability factor. The findings suggest that as ESG derivatives mature and attract deeper participation, pricing alignment with conventional benchmarks should improve, reducing the scope for persistent ESG-conventional futures spreads.

title: AIM (Adaptive, Inclusive, Moral) Political Economy: Introduction and Applications
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: AIM (Adaptive, Inclusive, Moral) Political Economy: Introduction and Applications
detail.abstract: The polycrisis marks a moment of global disruption, but it also opens a rare opportunity for intellectual transformation – what Yuen Yuen Ang calls polytunity. This essay introduces AIM (Adaptive, Inclusive, Moral) Political Economy as a paradigm designed for a disrupted, multipolar world. AIM replaces the industrial-colonial worldview that has long shaped political economy, challenging its mechanical assumptions, Eurocentric benchmarks, and claims of neutrality. AIM did not emerge recently; its core ideas and applications were already present in Ang’s earlier books, How China Escaped the Poverty Trap (2016) and China’s Gilded Age (2020), but misclassified due to structural erasure that confine non-Western scholarship to the realm of “exceptional cases.” Drawing on How China Escaped the Poverty Trap, Ang demonstrates AIM in action: development as a coevolutionary process in complex economic systems, and meta-institutions as higher-order designs that enable state-market coevolution. The essay concludes by situating AIM as a generative research paradigm – one whose roots lie in past work and whose canopy extends across ongoing projects in comparative corruption, fiscal capacity, and policy communication. AIM not only offers a compass for the current age of disruption, it extends an invitation to collectively build a more adaptive, pluralistic, and reflexive political economy.

title: Before the Allocation: An NGX Market Structure Framework for the Dangote Refinery Pan-African Listing

detail.title: Before the Allocation: An NGX Market Structure Framework for the Dangote Refinery Pan-African Listing
detail.abstract: The planned listing of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE on the NigerianExchange (NGX) main board represents the largest capital market event in the exchange's history. With a free float of up to 10% of a refinery valued at approximately 50 billion, the implied offering of roughly 5 billion will test the absorptive capacity of the Nigerian equity market in ways that have no precedent at this scale. This note is not a valuation analysis. It is the pre-listing market structure framework that international allocators require to quantify NGX-specific risks before committing capital. We address three empirical questions in causal sequence: what price gap investors should expect between the Lagos listing and international entry points; whether the asset's USD- denominated dividend genuinely hedges an international investor against naira risk; and whether NGX has sufficient liquidity depth to absorb a free float of this magnitude within a reasonable investment horizon. Drawing on 2,916 common trading days of Seplat Energy's dual NGX–LSE listing as an empirical prior, a proxy revenue model anchored on publicly available refinery margin data, and weekly NGX turnover observations, we quantify each risk dimension with full methodological transparency. Our central findings are: an expected NGX discount of approximately 13.2% to international pricing, within a projected band of −7.1%to −21.1%; a base-case USD dividend yield of 0.23% at normalised crack spreads that falls to zero under current depressed margin conditions; and a free-float absorption horizon of 57 to 143 weeks at observed participation rates. Allocation decisions made without this framework underwrite unquantified structural risk.

detail.abstract: This paper presents findings from a structured naturalistic observational study conducted in urban public environments in Lodz, Poland, between 2020 and 2026. Drawing on more than 2,000 recorded behavioral episodes involving children aged 1.5 to 13 years, their caregivers, and adults in shared public space, the study examines the conditions under which aggressive and boundary-violating behavior is transmitted, reinforced, and institutionally tolerated across all levels of the social system-from child to caregiver to educational institution to supervisory authority to national ombudsman. The central structural finding is that a dominance hierarchy, rather than a normative rule system, functions as the operative organizing principle of social interaction at every level of the observed system. Those with greater behavioral aggression or institutional authority displace those with less, through bodily pressure, volume, or evaluative power-not through agreed rules. Approximately 30 percent of observed adults and children violate boundaries without apparent awareness that such boundaries exist; a further comparable proportion restrains itself only under perceived surveillance. The study introduces the Boundary Regulation Index (BRI) as an observational measure capturing four dimensions of boundary functioning in public peer environments. A secondary finding is the acquired behavioral camouflage pattern among developmentally advanced children-a learned regulatory suppression strategy distinct from clinical developmental presentations and carrying specific diagnostic implications. Two structurally distinct but developmentally convergent socialization patterns are identified: permissive-aggressive and victim-oriented suppressive, both producing environments in which boundary-maintenance capacity fails to develop. The study documents systematic non-response and active legitimacy-based suppression by institutional actors across the full institutional chain, including the Commissioner for Children's Rights. The findings are corroborated by national statistical data and aligned with the developmental time-lag hypothesis: the population-level outcomes currently documented in Polish adolescents are temporally consistent with the regulatory suppression of the cohort that was 2 to 9 years old during the study period. The paper is situated within evolutionary neuroscience, developmental psychology, institutional theory, and behavioral economics, and is analyzed through the Psychoeconomic Resilience Model (PRM).

title: Navigating Adversity: A Systematic Review of Rural Livelihood Challenges in Somaliland

detail.title: Navigating Adversity: A Systematic Review of Rural Livelihood Challenges in Somaliland
detail.abstract: This systematic review aimed to synthesize the extant literature on the multifaceted challenges confronting rural livelihoods in Somaliland. Following the PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive search of academic databases and grey literature sources was conducted, identifying relevant studies published between 1991 and 2023. The review identified and analyzed four deeply interconnected thematic challenges: (1) Environmental and Climatic Shocks, including intensifying droughts, water scarcity, and pest outbreaks; (2) Economic and Livelihood Constraints, characterized by an over-reliance on pastoralism, limited diversification, and financial exclusion; (3) Political and Institutional Fragilities, rooted in non-recognition and limited state capacity; and (4) Social and Infrastructural Deficits, manifesting as crippling deficits in healthcare, education, and roads. The synthesis revealed that these themes form a vicious, self-reinforcing cycle of vulnerability, whereby a shock in one domain exacerbates pressures in another, trapping communities in a state of protracted crisis. The study concluded that the complex and synergistic nature of these adversities necessitates a fundamental shift away from siloed, short-term interventions towards integrated, multi-sectoral resilience-building approaches that are mindful of Somaliland's unique socio-political context. The review also highlighted significant gaps in the literature, pointing to avenues for future research.

title: Recognizing the Exceptional, Ignoring the Everyday: a Qualitative Study of Work Recognition Among Paramedics
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Recognizing the Exceptional, Ignoring the Everyday: a Qualitative Study of Work Recognition Among Paramedics
detail.abstract: The paramedic profession is undergoing a significant transformation driven by sociodemographic changes and evolving healthcare needs. As the profession shifts away from its historically transport-focused role toward more complex clinical, psychosocial and non-urgent transport, little is known about how organizations recognize these tasks. This study examines how paramedics perceive work recognition that manifests in their daily professional activities. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-one paramedics from five prehospital organizations in Quebec, Canada. Data were analyzed using an abductive thematic approach to capture both concept-driven and emergent dimensions of recognition. Findings show that recognition is largely absent from daily interactions and centers almost exclusively on rare, life-saving events. This outcome-based focus reinforces the gap between Work-as-Imagined and Work-as-Done, leaving everyday clinical and psychosocial work invisible. Furthermore, the public celebration of heroic acts may inadvertently exacerbate their emotional burden by requiring paramedics to revisit traumatic events. These results highlight the need for recognition practices that better reflect the realities of paramedic work and acknowledge the full range of contributions that shape everyday practice.

detail.abstract: The first three papers in this series established why the Human Layer matters, how to build it, and how to measure it. This paper addresses the question those papers raise but do not answer: if the evidence for augmentation over automation is this consistent, why does capital continue to flow toward replacement? The answer is not that executives are irrational. It is that the current incentive architecture makes removing the human layer structurally rational at the individual and organizational level, while externalizing the costs to a later period, a different line item, and often a different team. This paper identifies three capital incentive structures driving organizations toward automation: venture capital pricing dynamics, AI vendor pricing model evolution, and executive performance measurement. It introduces the concept of organizational automation bias: the systematic institutional tendency to overweight visible, near-term automation benefits and underweight deferred oversight costs. It then documents the three forces now collapsing the temporal gap that makes this externalization possible: regulatory enforcement becoming actualized, insurance and liability pricing beginning to incorporate AI risk, and institutional market access emerging as a gating function rather than a compliance aspiration. The paper closes with an empirically grounded argument, drawn from the SOX, GDPR, and ISO 27001 precedents, that the Human Layer Score introduced in Paper 3 is positioned to function as a capital markets signal for organizations operating in regulated, trust-dependent environments, and that governance infrastructure of this kind has historically been acquired most advantageously in the window before enforcement concentrates the market toward already-compliant actors.

title:
Preventive Healthcare as Fiscal Infrastructure: 
Public Nutrition Hubs and the Political Economy of U.S. Chronic Disease Costs

detail.title:
Preventive Healthcare as Fiscal Infrastructure: 
Public Nutrition Hubs and the Political Economy of U.S. Chronic Disease Costs

detail.abstract:
U.S. healthcare reform debates concentrate on insurance coverage, drug prices, hospital billing,
and administrative costs. These remain central. Yet the existing federal nutrition policy
architecture — WIC, SNAP-Ed, the Healthy Food Financing Initiative, Farm to School, and
federal school meal standards — leaves a specific institutional layer unfilled: there is no general-
population public prepared-meal infrastructure that could function as community-facing
preventive capacity. This paper argues that this institutional vacuum is a relevant policy variable
for U.S. chronic disease cost trajectories, and proposes one design — Public Nutrition Hub
Networks — for testing what filling it might do.
The contribution of this paper is not the claim that food affects health, which is well established,
nor that procurement has been absent from nutrition policy. The contribution is threefold and
narrower. First, it specifies a procurement-as-coalition mechanism that converts potential local-
restaurant opposition into structured supplier-network participation, drawing on public
procurement scholarship on procurement as a policy instrument (McCrudden, 2004; Mazzucato,
2018). Second, it formalizes adaptive nutrition standards as an implementation theory rather than
a compliance framework, addressing the documented plate-waste and uptake failures of stricter
school meal standards (Cohen et al., 2014; Bleich et al., 2018). Third, it specifies a school-adjacent
safety architecture as a precondition for community-facing public meal infrastructure in the U.S.
context, an issue largely absent from comparative public-meal scholarship that draws on systems
built before contemporary American school-security constraints.
The paper does not claim immediate healthcare savings or clinical efficacy independent of
evidence-based medicine. It proposes a long-horizon fiscal-prevention framework to be tested
through 3-5 year local pilots, with explicit treatment of identification threats, edge cases where
mitigation may fail, and documented negative lessons from comparator systems (Korea's 2011
free-meal political conflict; Japan's 2012 Chofu allergy fatality; Finnish school meal cost-quality
pressures). Its central argument is that one specific gap in the U.S. nutrition policy stack —
community-facing prepared-meal infrastructure — is testable, fiscally bounded, and politically
tractable if designed as a procurement coalition rather than as substitution for private food service.

title: PIDL: A Prompt Injection Detection Layer for LLM-Integrated Web Applications via Multi-Signal Semantic Analysis

detail.title: PIDL: A Prompt Injection Detection Layer for LLM-Integrated Web Applications via Multi-Signal Semantic Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research received no external funding.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a computer science systems design paper involving no human participants, patient data, or experimental studies requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded. No external grants or funding bodies supported this work.

detail.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) APIs are increasingly embedded into production web applications, creating a new class of security vulnerability: prompt injection. An adversarial user can embed instructions within their input that override the application's system prompt, exfiltrate confidential configuration, or redirect model behavior. No standardized, pre-execution defense mechanism currently exists for this threat class. We propose the Prompt Injection Detection Layer (PIDL), a stateless middleware component that intercepts user inputs before they are dispatched to an LLM API. PIDL executes a four-signal semantic analysis pipeline-detecting instruction-override patterns, semantic domain deviation, imperative density, and boundary marker presence-and computes a scalar Adversarial Intent Score (AIS) using a weighted linear combination. Inputs exceeding a configurable threshold are routed to a four-transformation sanitization stage before dispatch. PIDL is modelagnostic, requires no modification to the underlying LLM, and is designed to operate within a < 100ms latency budget for inputs up to 4,096 tokens. We describe the system architecture, signal formulations, scoring rationale, and sanitization transformations, and discuss deployment considerations. PIDL provides a principled, auditable foundation for prompt injection defense that complements existing alignment techniques.

title:
The Ontological Reduction of the Village Republic: 
Statutory Capture, Constitutional Inversion, and the Future of Article 371A

detail.title:
The Ontological Reduction of the Village Republic: 
Statutory Capture, Constitutional Inversion, and the Future of Article 371A
detail.abstract: This paper forms part of an ongoing series examining the constitutional, statutory, and institutional foundations of governance in Nagaland. It is offered as a contribution to critical public reasoning, an invitation to interrogate the legal architectures that shape our collective life and to consider how they may be strengthened to protect both community autonomy and democratic accountability. The analysis that follows emerges from a recent and rigorous public discourse on the relationship between Article 371A and the Nagaland Village Councils (NVC) Act of 1978. It is presented as a critical position paper intended to facilitate intellectual dialogue, systemic reflection, and informed public engagement. The arguments are grounded in a close reading of primary statutory texts and the constitutional framework of Article 371A of the Constitution of India. This work should not be read as a critique of any individual or institution, but as a structural inquiry into the frameworks within which they operate. Its purpose is not to undermine administrative practice, but to illuminate the gaps between constitutional promise and statutory reality, and to encourage thoughtful dialogue on how those gaps may be bridged. It is an independent intellectual exercise undertaken to safeguard the integrity of our ancestral institutions, ensuring they are preserved not merely in name or form, but protected in function and essence. This inquiry focuses specifically on the institutional and sovereign identity of the Village Republic. For a detailed examination of the broader legislative failures concerning resource management, dead capital, and fiscal agency under Section 12 of the Act, readers are referred to the author's companion policy paper, From Veto to Guarantee: Why Nagaland Must Author Its Own Rights. Readers are encouraged to engage with this work as a platform for discussion, critique, and collaborative thinking toward a more coherent, community-anchored governance architecture.

title: AML Observability: Rethinking Transaction Monitoring as a Debuggable Compliance System An Architectural Position Paper with a Larger Synthetic Evaluation
