detail.title: An Enterprise Architecture-Based AI TRiSM Framework for DataPrivacy Compliance Monitoring in National Cybersecurity Agencies

keywords.keywords: Artificial intelligenceAI TRiSMCompliance MonitoringCybersecurity AgencyData PrivacyEnterprise ArchitectureGovernance

detail.abstract: Organisations face escalating challenges in maintaining data privacy compliance amid evolving regulatory requirements, proliferating cyberthreats, and rapidly growing data volumes. Traditional compliance approaches remain largely manual, fragmented, and reactive, limiting scalability and real-time responsiveness. This study develops an Enterprise Architecture (EA)-driven Artificial Intelligence Trust, Risk, and Security Management (AI TRiSM) framework to enhance data privacy compliance monitoring within national cybersecurity agencies. Adopting a qualitative interpretivist approach, the study conducted semi-structured interviews with five domain experts from CyberSecurity Malaysia’s Information Security Management and Assurance Department. Data were analysed using six-phase thematic analysis via ATLAS.ti, and thematic saturation was reached within the five expert sessions. The findings reveal four key architectural layers: model monitoring, ModelOps, AI application security, and model privacy, with governance emerging as a cross-cutting enabler across all layers. These components are integrated into a structured multi-layered framework aligned with EA domains to support proactive compliance monitoring, real-time risk detection, and improved operational efficiency. The framework contributes by bridging the gap between AI governance and enterprise architecture, offering a systematic and scalable approach to privacy compliance in high-risk cybersecurity environments. The study provides both theoretical insights into AI-enabled compliance architectures and practical guidance for national-level agencies seeking to strengthen privacy governance. Future research is recommended to validate the framework across different sectors and through quantitative or longitudinal approaches.

title: Physics-Informed Dual-Branch Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Variable-Obstacle Turbulent Backward-Facing Step Flows
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian University of Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Dalian University of Technology

detail.title: Physics-Informed Dual-Branch Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Variable-Obstacle Turbulent Backward-Facing Step Flows
detail.abstract: Accurately predicting turbulent flows over variable geometries remains challenging because geometric changes can simultaneously alter the mean-flow structure, separation behavior, and associated Reynolds-stress fields. This study develops a hierarchical closure-coupled physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (HCC-PIKAN) for turbulent-flow prediction over variable geometries. The framework adopts a closure-coupled dual-branch architecture. A mean-flow branch first predicts pressure and velocity, and the predicted mean-flow variables are then used, together with the original geometry and flow inputs, to condition a turbulence-closure branch for Reynolds-stress prediction. This design introduces an explicit architecture-level link between mean-flow prediction and turbulence-closure modeling. Compact geometric features are extracted using a self-attention-based geometry encoder, and a two-stage training strategy is adopted to improve optimization stability. To enhance physical consistency, nondimensional continuity and momentum residuals with Reynolds-stress-divergence terms are enforced through automatic differentiation, while supervised and physics losses are dynamically balanced. Backward-facing-step configurations with variable obstacles are used as representative validation cases. Numerical results show that HCC-PIKAN outperforms the baseline physics-informed neural network and the single-network physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network. The best model achieves a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.012670, a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.006722, and a coefficient of determination of 0.9968, reducing RMSE and MAE by about 29.9% and 31.2%, respectively, relative to the baseline model. The framework also produces lower validation equation residuals and more compact residual distributions, demonstrating improved predictive accuracy and equation-level physical consistency for turbulent-flow surrogate modeling.

title: Too hot to work? Effect of temperature on intra-day work time​
affiliations: Department of Econometrics and OR Tilburg University, Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research and Tilburg University

detail.title: Too hot to work? Effect of temperature on intra-day work time​
detail.abstract: Rising temperatures due to climate change pose significant challenges to how much and how effectively individuals can work, particularly in low- and middle-income countries such as India, where exposure to extreme heat is becoming more common. While existing research documents adverse effects of heat on labor outcomes, little is known about how individuals adjust their work patterns within a day. This study examines the impact of ambient temperature on time allocation, with a focus on intraday substitution of time spent on paid work. The study uses nationally representative data from the 2019 Indian Time Use Survey combined with high-frequency temperature data measured at 30-minute intervals. We estimate the effect of temperature on total daily time spent on paid work and on the likelihood of working during specific periods of the day. Our results show that extreme heat has limited effects on overall daily work hours but leads to substantial intraday reallocation of labor. Individuals shift work from the hottest periods midday toward early morning or late evening. This pattern is primarily driven by younger men and workers in self-employed or agricultural jobs, who have greater flexibility in their schedules and are more exposed to ambient heat. In contrast, salaried workers reduce work during peak heat without compensatory increases at other times. These findings highlight the importance of flexible work arrangements and targeted heat-mitigation policies to sustain productivity and worker well-being in a warming climate.

title: Quantifying the Environmental & Economic Impacts of Integrated Organic Waste Management in a Tropical Urbanizing Ecotourism Region
affiliations: Universidade Federal de Pernambuco (UFPE), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Costa Rica, University of Costa Rica, Universidade Federal Rural de Pernambuco (UFRPE) and West Virginia University

detail.title: Quantifying the Environmental & Economic Impacts of Integrated Organic Waste Management in a Tropical Urbanizing Ecotourism Region
detail.abstract: Given the finite lifespan of traditional landfills, alternative waste management systems are needed to reduce environmental impacts, promote resource recovery, and support a circular economy. This study evaluated the environmental and economic sustainability of four organic waste treatment scenarios in Monteverde, Costa Rica, analyzing collection and transportation (C&T) routes and operational systems of: 1) landfill, 2) municipal centralized composting, 3) municipal centralized anaerobic co-digestion (ACD), and 4) ACD in a private cheese factory. Methodology integrated geoprocessing, Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), and Life Cycle Cost Analysis (LCCA). Results showed that C&T accounted for over 90% of Global Warming Potential (GWP) and Eutrophication Potential. Combined C&T and operations revealed that Scenario 1 had the highest negative impact on Marine Eutrophication Potential (MEP) (1,74E-4 t Neq), while Scenario 2 caused the highest GWP and Freshwater Eutrophication Potential (FEP) due to co-substrate transport (12.23 t CO2eq and 3.09E-4 t Peq, respectively). Although Scenario 3 minimized impacts across all environmental categories (10.44 t CO2eq, 2.68E-4 t Peq, and 4.19E-5 t Neq), it incurred the highest cost per ton (US$ 437) due to structural complexity. Conversely, Scenario 4 had the lowest cost per ton (US$ 164). Over a 10-year LCCA period, Scenario 2 required the highest municipal financial incentive (US$ 1,803,159), whereas Scenario 4 required the lowest (US$ 648,468). Consequently, selecting the most sustainable waste management system requires a multi-criteria approach to navigate trade-offs. Thus, decision-making must extend beyond financial costs alone to mitigate transport impacts, evaluate renewable fuels, and incorporate social effects.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and ensemble learners for predicting brine-hydrogen/cushion-gas interfacial tension in underground hydrogen storage
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nazarbayev University, Kaunas University of Technology, Shiraz University, Nazarbayev University, Nazarbayev University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Nazarbayev University

detail.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and ensemble learners for predicting brine-hydrogen/cushion-gas interfacial tension in underground hydrogen storage
detail.abstract: Underground hydrogen storage is a promising method for addressing the energy gap. Nonetheless, hydrogen migration is the main challenge of efficient storage, especially in saline aquifer targets. Gas-brine interfacial tension (IFT) is a critical parameter that controls capillary forces and optimizes the injection cycle conditions to enhance the efficacy of underground hydrogen storage on a field scale. This study aims to apply categorical boosting regressor (CB), decision tree, extra trees regressor, Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN), random forest, and extreme gradient boosting machine learning techniques to extensive experimental studies. Specifically, 2803 data points are used to predict the IFT with the influence of vast ranges of pressure, temperature, salinity, ∆ρ, and working gas (H2) with different cushion gases. Statistical description (box plots, pair plot, and Spearman correlation coefficient) and model evaluation graphs were applied to study the dataset and the performance of the applied models. The results demonstrate that KAN and CB have superior performance with total R2 of 0.9979 and 0.9976, and root mean square errors of 0.4828 mN.m-1 and 0.5097 mN.m-1, respectively. The KAN model provides an accurate data-driven tool for estimating gas-brine IFT under underground hydrogen storage conditions and may support future screening, sensitivity analysis, and reservoir-scale modeling of hydrogen storage systems. These findings highlight the potential of KAN-based modeling to provide reliable IFT estimates for gas-brine systems, supporting data-driven assessment and design of safer underground hydrogen storage operations.

detail.abstract: The AI Availability framework (González Castro 2026d) operationalises AI Availability at the brand level, scoring each brand's surfacing rate, prominence, and favourable representation in generative AI responses to category-relevant queries. Most major firms operate multi-brand corporate portfolios in which brand-level outcomes aggregate to the corporate level along pathways that depend on brand architecture. This paper specifies the aggregation logic for the four standard architecture types of the Aaker spectrum — branded house, sub-brand, endorsed brand, house of brands (Aaker and Joachimsthaler 2000) — and develops a coupling-coefficient formalism that makes architecture-aware corporate AIAS aggregation tractable. The paper states the cross-architecture comparison hypothesis (H_arch): for matched categories, branded-house and house-of-brands corporations face systematically different distributions of AI-mediation risk, with branded-house structures concentrating the risk in single-point-of-failure form and house-of-brands structures distributing the risk in hidden-cell form. Three governance implications follow: governance locus by architecture, the cross-brand cannibalisation question unique to multi-brand portfolios, and corporate AIAS reporting at the level of analysis appropriate for the architecture. The paper specifies the matched-pair comparative empirical design required to test H_arch and registers the design as a research-agenda priority.

detail.abstract: Brand-strength scoring frameworks that underpin brand valuation — Interbrand's Brand Strength Score, Brand Finance's Brand Strength Index, Kantar BrandZ, and comparable models — were developed before generative AI became a material intermediary in brand discovery. The frameworks measure the brand-equity assets that classical theory identifies as drivers of brand value, but they do not measure whether and how those assets are surfaced by AI systems consulted during category episodes. This paper proposes an additive AI Availability factor appended to existing brand-strength scores: BS(adjusted) = BS(traditional) + α · AIAS where AIAS is the AI Availability Score (González Castro 2026d, 2026c) and α ∈ [0, 1] is a category-specific weight calibrated annually against the observed share of category purchase decisions routed through AI-mediated retrieval. The additive form preserves backward compatibility with historical brand-strength scores, is interpretively transparent (the AI Availability score is reported alongside traditional factor scores rather than buried inside a weighting coefficient), and maps onto existing valuation methodologies in which each factor has defined evaluation criteria, scoring bands, and explicable logic. Three deprecation triggers are specified under which the factor is retired for a category, restoring the classical brand-strength model. The proposal complements rather than displaces classical brand-strength theory; the empirical calibration of α and the predictive validity of the adjusted score against subsequent brand-value movements are the next research priorities.

title: Dynamic Spatial Panel Data Analysis of Inbound Accommodation Demand in Japan: Estimation and Forecasting

detail.title: Dynamic Spatial Panel Data Analysis of Inbound Accommodation Demand in Japan: Estimation and Forecasting
detail.abstract: This study examines the spatial dependence structure of inbound foreign tourist accommodation demand using monthly panel data for 47 Japanese prefectures (January 2007-December 2019), and evaluates the forecasting utility of spatial models. We estimate spatial Durbin error models (SDEM) and dynamic spatial Durbin models (SDM), employing foreign overnight stays from the Japan Tourism Agency's Accommodation Survey as the dependent variable, with the USD/JPY exchange rate, WTI crude oil price, and city-level consumer price index as explanatory variables. Bayesian spatial model selection consistently favors SDEM, and the dynamic SDM estimation yields statistically significant spatial autoregressive parameters, temporal lags, and negative spillover effects from neighboring prefectures' price levels. Comparing two spatial weight matrices, a travel-time distance matrix based on the National Passenger Flow Survey substantially outperforms the traditional contiguity matrix in model fit. Both matrices detect a significant negative spillover effect of neighboring CPI (W • cpi), but the effect size under the travel-time matrix (-0.084, 𝑡 =-2.26) is approximately 18 times larger than under the Queen contiguity matrix (-0.005, 𝑡 =-2.86), demonstrating that the choice of spatial weight matrix is not merely a technical decision but a substantive analytical choice that determines the magnitude of detected spatial spillovers. In the forecasting analysis, a holdout comparison of six models (2018-2019) reveals that the introduction of temporal lags dramatically improves forecast accuracy, while the additional contribution of spatial structure remains limited. Under seasonal differencing, all models beat the seasonal naïve benchmark (MASE < 1), yet the gap between spatial models and the dynamic fixed-effects model is marginal. These results suggest that spatial dependence is essential for understanding the mechanisms of inbound accommodation demand but does not directly translate into practical short-term forecast improvement, consistent with the findings of Jiao et al. (2021).

title: Interpreting Sensory Experience in Customer-generated Text: A Large Language Model (LLM) Approach

detail.title: Interpreting Sensory Experience in Customer-generated Text: A Large Language Model (LLM) Approach

detail.abstract: Sensory dimension is a central component of how consumers evaluate products and services, and online reviews offer a rich record of how these experiences are described. Prior research has used lexicon-based text analysis to extract sensory cues from customer language by mapping words to predefined sensory dictionaries and examining their effects on ratings. However, such approaches rely on fixed word–sense mappings and struggle to capture the context-dependent nature of sensory language. A context-sensitive approach using large language models (LLMs) to interpret sensory language in customer reviews is introduced. Validated against human coders and lexicon-based methods across 82,350 restaurant reviews, the LLM achieves substantially higher reliability by capturing implicit and context-dependent sensory references. While lexicon-based approaches infer senses from predefined word categories, LLMs infer which sensory modalities are most likely activated given the linguistic context. Leveraging this approach, this research moves beyond identifying sensory cues to examine how sensory experiences are used in evaluation. The findings suggest that sensory modalities exhibit markedly different associations with ratings when considered in isolation, but these differences are largely explained by the evaluative contexts in which sensory experiences are expressed. Different sensory modalities are disproportionately associated with positive versus negative evaluations, with some primarily used to express hedonic assessments and others more frequently invoked as diagnostic cues in negative evaluations. This study demonstrates how LLMs can be used to interpret customer experience from consumer text and provides a framework for uncovering the evaluative roles of sensory attributes that can be generalised across product types.

detail.abstract: Brand erasure (Figueira, 2026a, 2026b) named the failure mode of brand theory in AI-mediated markets-the systematic suppression of brand identity inside synthesized answers and completed agentic actions. This paper develops the corresponding positive construct: Brand Legibility, the degree to which a brand is recognizable, parseable, and attributable by the AI systems that mediate consumer experience. We position Brand Legibility as the latent-substrate counterpart of brand salience (Romaniuk & Sharp, 2004) and the operational property whose absence produces erasure. We introduce the Semantic Equity Index (SEI) as the quantitative measure of legibility and the Brand Legibility Framework as the operating model that integrates Answer Engine Optimization, Generative Engine Optimization, and Agentic Optimization as three coordinated layers. We close with the Brand Erasure Audit as the measurement protocol that operationalizes the framework, and with implications for brand-equity theory, marketing organizations, and the governance of attribution.

title: 'An Empirical Analysis of the Effectiveness of Digital Marketing Strategies in the UAE Real Estate Business Sector'
affiliations: Manipal GlobalNxt University, Malaysia and Manipal GlobalNxt University Malaysia

detail.title: 'An Empirical Analysis of the Effectiveness of Digital Marketing Strategies in the UAE Real Estate Business Sector'
detail.abstract: In UAE, property developers, real estate agencies, and brokers, leverage digital platforms to showcase their listings, targeting local, and international buyers and tenants. As of January 2025, active social media identities in the UAE are reported at ~11.3 million, approximately 100% of the population, underscoring the pervasiveness of digital touch points across segments and nationalities (Data Reportal, 2025). The core problem is that UAE real estate businesses lack empirical clarity regarding the actual effectiveness of digital marketing strategies. Therefore, there is a clear need for systematic empirical search to examine the impact of digital marketing concepts in the UAE real estate sector. This study adopted a cross-sectional survey research design, where data were collected at a single point of time in the year 2025 from business customers operating across various segments of the UAE real estate sector. The survey was administered through multiple channels, including email distribution, social media platforms, and direct communication through personal visits or phone calls and valid data were collected from 330 respondents. One sample t-test was conducted to test the hypotheses formulated for the study. The results proved that the all the four variables under study, viz., Search Engine Optimization (SEO), Social Media Marketing (SMM), Content Marketing (CTM), and E-mail Marketing (EMM) are high-performing, with SMM being the most significant driver among the tested variables. By 2026, UAE real estate marketing has matured into an integrated, high-tech system, where SMM drives high-intent sales, and immersive content is essential for trust. The UAE real estate market keeps moving fast, and in 2026 social media sits at the centre of property search and sale. It connects with buyers from Asia, Europe, and GCC. Social Media makes it easier to showcase properties clearly, and it allows quickreal conversations with potential buyers.

title: NEMESIS-Edge: A Neuromorphic Multimodal Edge Architecture or Energy-Efficient Real-Time Perception in UAV and Healthcare Systems

keywords.keywords: Neuromorphic computingEdge AIMultimodal perceptionEnergy-efficient AIReal-time inferenceUAV systemsHealthcare AISpiking neural networks

detail.abstract: Neuromorphic computing has emerged as a promising paradigm forenabling energy-efficient and low-latency intelligence at the edge, partic-ularly for applications requiring real-time multimodal perception. Thispaper presents NEMESIS-Edge, a novel neuromorphic multimodal edgearchitecture designed to integrate heterogeneous sensory data under strictresource constraints. The proposed framework leverages spiking neuralnetworks (SNNs) for event-driven processing, significantly reducing com-putational overhead compared to conventional deep learning approaches.At the core of the architecture is SpikeFusion-X, a spike-domain multi-modal fusion algorithm that preserves temporal dynamics while enablingefficient cross-modal interaction. The framework supports multiple sens-ing modalities, including RGB visual data, polarimetric infrared sensing,and physiological signals, making it suitable for both UAV-based percep-tion and healthcare monitoring applications. A hardware-aware designstrategy is incorporated to ensure compatibility with neuromorphic pro-cessors and edge devices by considering sparsity, quantization, and mem-ory efficiency constraints. Experimental evaluation is conducted using a benchmark-driven method-ology aligned with emerging neuromorphic evaluation standards. Resultsdemonstrate that NEMESIS-Edge achieves up to 6× lower latency and 8×higher energy efficiency compared to baseline approaches while maintain-ing competitive perception accuracy. Additional ablation and robustnessanalyses further validate the effectiveness of the proposed spike-domainfusion mechanism under heterogeneous sensing conditions.Overall, NEMESIS-Edge provides a scalable and efficient frameworkfor real-time neuromorphic edge intelligence across diverse multimodalapplication domains.

title: Energy and carbon routing in hydrothermal lignocellulosic biomass conversion: an uncertainty-aware machine-learning framework

detail.title: Energy and carbon routing in hydrothermal lignocellulosic biomass conversion: an uncertainty-aware machine-learning framework
detail.abstract: Reliable assessment of hydrothermal lignocellulosic biomass conversion requires quantitative prediction of how feedstock mass, chemical energy, and carbon partition among bio-oil, solid residues, aqueous products, and gases under heterogeneous feedstock, solvent, catalyst, and severity conditions. We constructed a harmonized database of 3,693 HTL/HTC experiments from 187 scientific papers and 433 different biomass samples, with temperatures up to ∼ 600 ◦C and maximum residence times of up to 1,200 min. From this literature-scale dataset, we developed an uncertainty-aware machine-learning framework for predicting mass partitioning, energy and carbon allocation, and higher heating value (HHV) of condensed phases. Among the tree-ensemble regression methods examined, Random Forest (RF) provided the most stable cross-target compromise, with test R2 values for product yields around 0.8, energy/carbon allocation metrics between 0.8 and 0.9, and bio-oil HHV around 0.7 with root-mean-squared error ∼ 2–3 MJkg−1. The model recovers established severity, solvent, and composition trends while identifying regions where predictions are well supported or weakly constrained. SHAP attributions are interpreted as model-conditional associations: liquid-phase outcomes depend strongly on solvent and operating conditions, whereas solid-phase HHVs are more associated with feedstock carbon and ash content. Ensemble and conformal uncertainty methods distinguish relative epistemic uncertainty from calibrated scenario bounds. The framework is intended for uncertainty-aware process screening, scenario bounding, and experimental prioritization rather than unqualified point optimization in poorly represented regimes.

title: ASSESSMENTS OF THE PRIMARY FACTORS AFFECTING DRIVING SPEED AND THE VIOLATION OF THE SPEED LIMIT BY DRIVERS IN ADDIS ABABA
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: ASSESSMENTS OF THE PRIMARY FACTORS AFFECTING DRIVING SPEED AND THE VIOLATION OF THE SPEED LIMIT BY DRIVERS IN ADDIS ABABA
detail.abstract: Purpose: The primary aim of this research is to establish the key factors influencing driving speed and the level of compliance among drivers with posted speed limits (PSLs) in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.Design/Methodology/Approach: - A mixed-methods design was employed. Spot speed data were collected on various types of roads (arterials, sub-arterials, collectors, and locals), and 450 drivers were surveyed using convenience sampling. Multiple linear regression was utilized to investigate the effects on operating speed, while ordinal logistic regression modeled self-reported offenses as a function of driver demographics and attitudes.Findings: Results show that operating speeds are influenced by roadway characteristics (e.g., pedestrian activity, number of lanes) (p < 0.05). Driver demographics (gender, age, experience) are the primary predictors of violations. A basic knowledge-behavior gap exists, with most drivers being knowledgeable about speeding hazards but still violating limits. Commercial drivers most prominently cite income pressure as the primary reason for non-compliance, as adherence to PSLs would reduce their daily income.Practical Implications: The findings suggest that traditional safety countermeasures are insufficient. Multi-dimensional interventions incorporating engineering strategies (e.g., traffic calming), selective enforcement, and strategies to mitigate the economic pressures faced by commercial drivers need to be implemented by policymakers and traffic managers. Ignoring the economic dimension of speeding will compromise the effectiveness of safety programs.Originality/Value: This paper presents a novel, evidence-based perspective on speeding in a developing urban context by quantifying the significant role of economic pressure on commercial driver behavior, a factor that has been considerably overlooked in traditional safety research.

title: Unbundling Extension Access, Cassava Variety Adoption, and Household Food Security in Nigeria: Evidence from the General Household Survey
affiliations: University of Ibadan Ibadan Nigeria and University of Ibadan, Ibadan, Nigeria

detail.title: Unbundling Extension Access, Cassava Variety Adoption, and Household Food Security in Nigeria: Evidence from the General Household Survey
detail.abstract: Agricultural extension systems in sub-Saharan Africa are increasingly evolving, yet evidence on whether access to extension services generates distinct welfare effects and through which pathways remain limited. This study operationalises extension access as via government agents, formal non-government sources, peer and cooperative networks, and digital platforms. It examines their independent effects on improved cassava variety adoption and household food security among 1,524 cassava-farming households in Nigeria, using nationally representative data from the General Household Survey–Panel Wave 5 (2023/24). Employing survey-weighted probit and ordinary least squares models alongside bootstrap causal mediation analysis, the total effect of extension access on food security is decomposed into an indirect component operating through improved variety adoption and a direct component reflecting all other pathways. First, no extension channel robustly increases improved cassava variety adoption; peer and cooperative extension is associated with a significant reduction in adoption probability of 14.4 percentage points. Second, extension channels improve household dietary diversity significantly as each additional channel accessed is associated with 0.25 additional food groups at the planting wave and 0.39 at the harvest wave. However, the proportion of this effect mediated through variety adoption is consistently below one percent across all specifications, indicating that direct knowledge and market access pathways dominate. Third, female-headed households have near-zero extension access across all channels. These results challenge the use of variety adoption as the primary metric for extension impact evaluation, identify direct agronomic knowledge transfer and market access as the dominant welfare-generating mechanisms of extension.

title: Turboexpander or Regulator? Probabilistic Exergy Destruction Mapping with Controlled Preheating for Natural Gas Pressure Reduction – a Monte Carlo study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Turboexpander or Regulator? Probabilistic Exergy Destruction Mapping with Controlled Preheating for Natural Gas Pressure Reduction – a Monte Carlo study
detail.abstract: Natural gas pressure-reduction stations conventionally dissipate the exergy of the incoming gas through throttling valves. Replacing these valves with turboexpanders can recover useful work, but the need for preheating to avoid hydrate formation creates a trade-off that may offset this benefit. This study presents a rigorous second-law comparison of regulator and turboexpander systems using a controlled, minimum-energy preheating strategy. All thermodynamic properties are computed with the AGA-8 equation of state to ensure high accuracy. A novel comparative exergy destruction parameter Δ is defined, and three operational scenarios are identified. A Monte Carlo simulation with 50,000 samples spanning realistic inlet pressures (300–1000 psi), temperatures (10–50 °C), and heater efficiencies (0.50–0.95) maps the probabilistic performance. Results show that the turboexpander system destroys less total exergy than the regulator system in 30.7% of the investigated conditions. The preheater contributes, on average, 78.1% of the turboexpander system’s total exergy destruction, compared with only 4.3% for the regulator. An optimal inlet pressure exists for each inlet temperature that minimizes Δ; this inlet pressure increases with inlet temperature up to about 500 psi. The study provides a clear decision map: the turboexpander is second-law superior only in a well-defined region of moderate pressure, high inlet temperature, and high heater efficiency. These findings offer a quantitative basis for selecting stations where turboexpander installation is thermodynamically justified.

title: Is Circular the new Resilient? Rethinking EU Performance through a New Sustainable Resilience Index
affiliations: University of Prešov and University of Prešov

detail.title: Is Circular the new Resilient? Rethinking EU Performance through a New Sustainable Resilience Index
detail.abstract: As European countries face increasing environmental pressures, shifting geopolitical dynamics, and growing concerns over material dependency, the concept of sustainable resilience is gaining prominence in EU policy and academic discourse. Although the circular economy (CE) is widely recognised as a strategic response to resource and climate challenges, the empirical linkages between CE and economic resilience remain under-explored. This study constructs a Sustainable Resilience Index (SRI) for EU-26 countries over the period 2010–2022, integrating indicators across environmental pressures, circularity, innovation, and global economic integration. Using principal component analysis, the index captures multi-dimensional systemic resilience. The results reveal substantial cross-country heterogeneity, with SRI scores ranging from near-zero in Romania to above 90 in Denmark and Luxembourg, and a pronounced north-west to south-east geographic gradient persisting throughout the observation period. Results demonstrate that productive and innovation capacities exert stronger influence on the SRI than circularity indicators. This suggests that while CE contributes to long-term resilience through reduced material dependence and import exposure, its role remains secondary to broader structural capacities. A gradual convergence in SRI scores is observed, driven primarily by improvements among lower-ranked countries, though the absolute gap between leaders and laggards remains substantial. The study offers a replicable framework for tracking sustainable resilience and provides policy-relevant insights for aligning CE strategies with structural capacity building, place-based development, and the EU's open strategic autonomy agenda.

title: From Hand Detachment to Mind Detachment A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Alienation in the Age of AI

detail.title: From Hand Detachment to Mind Detachment A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Alienation in the Age of AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil
declarations.funderStatement: Nil

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual distinction between two forms of detachment that have been conflated in critical theories of modernity and capitalism. Hand detachment refers to the process by which tools—information, resources, capital—leave the immediate control of their creators. This is a necessary condition for civilizational progress, from writing to money to the internet. Mind detachment refers to the qualitatively different process by which judgment itself leaves the human mind—the outsourcing of cognition to algorithms, but also, historically, to chiefs, kings, priests, and party leaders. While hand detachment expands the scope of human control across time and space, mind detachment corrodes the very boundary of the subject. The paper traces a spectrum of detachment (resources < information < capital → mind) and introduces a 2×3 matrix that distinguishes hand from mind detachment and traces their three-stage trajectory (S→I→S / W→G→W; I→S→I / G→W→G; I→I / G→G'). It argues that existing critical theories—from Marx to Weber to Zuboff—share a common blind spot: the conflation of hand detachment with mind detachment and the externalization of alienation. The paper then distinguishes capital alienation (H-II) from information alienation (M-II, M-III), showing that the latter presents a qualitatively different challenge: the subject may know but not care (M-II), or risk being bypassed altogether (M-III). The response is cognitive sovereignty: the subject's capacity to refuse the offloading of judgment, operationalized through three questions (identity, capability, responsibility) and requiring three institutional design principles (reversible, auditable, exitable). The paper concludes that hand detachment is irreversible but mind detachment can be defended—but only if the subject chooses to defend it, and only if institutions are designed to make that choice possible.

title: Corporate Labor Misconduct Risk: Evidence from 10-K Disclosures and Enforcement
affiliations: and Queen Mary, University of London, School of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Corporate Labor Misconduct Risk: Evidence from 10-K Disclosures and Enforcement
detail.abstract: We develop novel firm-level textual measures of corporate labor misconduct risk for U.S.-listed firms by combining 10-K risk disclosures with data on laborrelated violations and a comprehensive labor-risk dictionary. The measures capture distinct dimensions of misconduct related to benefit and wage violations, employment discrimination, and workplace safety breaches. They capture economically meaningful variation in labor misconduct risk, predicting subsequent enforcement actions, aligning with regulatory and industry patterns, and being associated with future stock return volatility. While realized stock returns show no significant labor risk premium, option-implied expected returns reveal a strong size pattern: the premium is positive for large firms but negative for small firms. Consistent with this, labor risk predicts enforcement outcomes across both size segments, indicating that markets incorporate labor risk into expected returns with heterogeneous pricing across firm size.

title: Debt is Not Leprosy—Mismanaged Debt is: A Development Finance Analysis of Nigeria's Fiscal Sustainability
affiliations: University of Lagos

detail.title: Debt is Not Leprosy—Mismanaged Debt is: A Development Finance Analysis of Nigeria's Fiscal Sustainability

contentType.other: a work in progress paper prepared for presentation at a conference

detail.abstract: Nigeria's expanding public debt profile has become a central point of national policy debate, catalysed by the Tinubu administration's assertion that "borrowing is not leprosy." This paper advances a structured counter-argument: public debt is not inherently destabilising; rather, it is the mismanagement of debt-characterised by consumption-driven borrowing, chronic underperformance of capital expenditure, and a persistently narrow tax base-that generates fiscal pathology. Drawing on data from Nigeria's Debt Management Office (DMO), the Federal Ministry of Finance, Budget and National Planning (FMFBNP), the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), and multilateral institutions including the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, this study analyses Nigeria's fiscal transformation between 2010 and 2025. Key findings reveal a structural divergence: total debt stock expanded by approximately 891% over the period while government retained revenue grew by only 258%. By 2024, Nigeria's debt service-to-revenue ratio stood at 69%-nearly double the 30-40% threshold recommended by the IMF and World Bank for developing economies. Capital expenditure execution in 2025 reached only 17.7% of allocation in the first three quarters. The paper proposes a threemetric diagnostic framework-comprising the Debt Service-to-Revenue Ratio, CAPEX Execution Rate, and Non-Oil Tax-to-GDP Ratio-as a more reliable indicator of fiscal sustainability than the conventional Debt-to-GDP ratio. The study concludes with evidence-based policy recommendations anchored on fiscal transparency, revenue resilience, and the golden rule of public borrowing: borrowed capital must generate returns commensurate with its cost.

title: Does Model Matter? Improving Permanency in Kinship Foster Care
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh, University of Pittsburgh, University of Pittsburgh, A Second Chance, Inc and A Second Chance, Inc

detail.title: Does Model Matter? Improving Permanency in Kinship Foster Care
detail.abstract: Kinship care has been widely promoted as a preferred placement strategy in child welfare; however, rigorous evaluations of specific kinship service models remain limited. This study examines whether participation in A Second Chance, Inc.’s (ASCI) Point-of-Contact (PoC) model is associated with improved placement stability and permanency outcomes compared to other kinship care services. Using administrative data from Allegheny County (2018-2023), the sample included 2,593 children placed in kinship care. Outcomes included placement disruptions, number of child welfare episodes, reentry into care, and permanency type, including Subsidized Permanent Legal Custodianship (SPLC). Results indicate that children served through the PoC model experienced significantly greater stability and improved permanency outcomes. Compared to children served by non-ASCI agencies, PoC participants had lower rates of reentry (37.4%vs.50.5%), fewer placement episodes, and fewer placement disruptions. While no significant differences were observed in adoption or reunification, children in the PoC model were significantly more likely to achieve permanency through SPLC. Additional analyses showed that placement with relative kin was associated with greater stability and a lower likelihood of reentry compared to non-relative (fictive) kin placements. Importantly, the advantages of the PoC model persisted even among children placed with relatives, suggesting that outcomes were not solely attributable to caregiver type. Findings suggest that structured, kin-first service models that integrate early intervention, triadic family engagement, and culturally responsive supports may enhance placement stability and promote sustainable permanency. These results have important implications for child welfare policy and practice, particularly in supporting kinship caregivers and addressing structural inequities.

title: A Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Accurate Daily Global Solar Radiation Estimation
affiliations: Moulay Ismail University, Moulay Ismail University, Moulay Ismail University, Moulay Ismail University and Abdelmalek Essaadi University

detail.title: A Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Accurate Daily Global Solar Radiation Estimation
detail.abstract: Accurate estimation of daily global solar radiation (H) is fundamental to the optimisation of energy and environmental systems, where meteorological-data-driven predictive models have emerged as powerful tools. However, model performance remains sensitive to the selection of input variables, architectural design, and the temporal parameters governing the learning process. This study addresses these challenges by developing and evaluating deep learning models for H prediction in Chafchaouen, Morocco, using historical meteorological data. Three model architectures are systematically compared: a baseline Variational Autoencoder (VAE) as well as two brand-new hybrid architectures, VAE-Reinforced-Transformer and LSTM-VAE-Transformer, proposed here for the first time in the field of solar radiation estimation. A key contribution of this work is the incorporation of evapotranspiration (ET) as an input feature alongside conventional meteorological variables (temperature, wind speed, and sunshine duration), a combination not previously explored for H estimation. The influence of temporal sequence length on prediction stability and accuracy is also rigorously investigated. The main objective is to quantify the impact of the ET parameter on learning capabilities and to rigorously evaluate the performance of the new hybrid models, as well as to analyse the influence of sequence length on the stability and accuracy of H’s predictions. The performance was evaluated using three standard statistical metrics: R², MAE, and RMSE. For the configuration using the TE parameter with a sequence length of 7, the LSTM-VAE-Transformer model achieved the best results on the test set (0.903278, 0.530526, and 0.705385, respectively), followed by the VAE-Reinforced-Transformer model (0.893009, 0.546215, and 0.741885). In contrast, the standard VAE model yielded significantly lower performance (0.803453, 0.801880, and 1.005533). These findings demonstrate that integrating ET as a predictor, combined with hybrid deep learning architectures and extended temporal sequences, substantially enhances the capacity to capture complex temporal dependencies and improves H estimation accuracy.

title: Selected Sectoral Contribution to Unemployment Reduction and Economic Growth in Nigeria
affiliations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, Kaduna State University and Nnamdi Azikiwe University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Selected Sectoral Contribution to Unemployment Reduction and Economic Growth in Nigeria
detail.abstract: This paper analysed the sectorial contribution of the Nigeria's economy to unemployment reduction for the period (1981-2016) using unemployment rate as a dependent variable while sectoral gross domestic product serves as the independent variables. The variables were tested to check whether they have unit root using Augmented Dickey-Fuller test. The result of the unit root test showed that the variables are integrated of different order. Based on the outcome of the unit root test, Autoregressive Distribution lag (ARDL) model was used to estimate the parameters of the model. The result of the ARDL short-run and long-run estimate revealed that art and entertainment sector, agricultural sector, educational sector and manufacturing sector statistically contribute to the reduction of unemployment in Nigeria both in the short-run and in the long-run at 5percent level, hence they create employment more than any other sector in Nigeria. While real estate sector and mining sector do not contribute to the reduction of unemployment both in the short-run and in the long-run. Based on the findings, this paper recommended that government should diversify the economy to enable greater growth and encourage employment generation in these sectors that shows positive signs of reducing youth unemployment and creating unemployment in Nigeria.

title: Capitalist Development and the Logic of Crisis: From the Natural and Monetary Cycle to a Structural-Interpretative Measure of Economic Fluctuations
affiliations: Universitas Prasetiya Mulya - School of Business and Economics

detail.title: Capitalist Development and the Logic of Crisis: From the Natural and Monetary Cycle to a Structural-Interpretative Measure of Economic Fluctuations
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a unified framework for understanding and measuring business cycles by integrating theoretical reconstruction with methodological innovation. Part I revisits and extends the Austrian Business Cycle Theory by introducing the concept of the natural cycle, defined as a form of fluctuation emerging endogenously from the dynamics of innovation, imitation, and expectation formation, even in the absence of monetary distortion. Drawing on the contributions of Friedrich Hayek, Joseph Schumpeter, and Ludwig Lachmann, the paper argues that crises are not merely the outcome of policy errors but are inherent to the temporal and interpretative nature of capitalist development. It distinguishes analytically between monetary cycles, driven by credit-induced miscoordination, and natural cycles, arising from the endogenous amplification of expectations through social imitation.

Building on this theoretical foundation, Part II addresses the measurement problem. It critiques GDP-centred approaches for their inability to capture the structural and forward-looking nature of cyclical processes and proposes the Structural Cycle and Coordination Index (SCCI) as an alternative framework. The SCCI operationalizes cyclical analysis through four pillars—production structure shifts, expectations and narrative temperature, monetary-financial stretch, and coordination strain—thus shifting the focus from aggregate output to the evolving coherence of economic plans.

By combining interpretative theory with transparent empirical design, the paper advances a conception of cycles as processes of coordination, misalignment, and recoordination, offering both a richer analytical lens and a practical tool for real-time economic diagnosis.

title: Two Contracts, Not Two Firms: The Manager-Priced SME Credit Contract in a Middle-Income Economy

detail.title: Two Contracts, Not Two Firms: The Manager-Priced SME Credit Contract in a Middle-Income Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of Interest
declarations.funderStatement: Banco Estado

detail.abstract: Why does the bank charge more when the numbers look better? Chilean small and medium-sized firms borrow less than large firms-a 39 percent debt-to-assets ratio against 55, and a 46 percent short-term-debt-to-sales ratio against 83-and present managers who are slightly older and more experienced than their large-firm counterparts (53.5 years against 51.1; 23 years of experience against 20). They pay, on the same data, an effective lending rate of approximately 6.2 percent against 4.4 percent for large firms-a 1.8-percentage-point premium that survives every direct balance-sheet control. The premium is the puzzle. We answer it by recognising that SME credit and large-firm credit are not points on a single size-of-firm curve: they are two distinct contractual regimes. The SME contract is a person-priced signature contract-a loan executed with a personal guarantee and underwritten on the owner's biography (age, education, experience, ownership share, family history). The large-firm contract is a balance-sheet-priced contract executed without a personal guarantee. Working with the Tercera Encuesta Longitudinal de Empresas (ELE-3)-approximately 2,174 SMEs and 3,299 large firms across twelve sectorswe estimate, side by side, the same five outcome equations on each subsample: total debt, short-term debt, long-term debt, the debt-to-assets ratio, and default. Manager characteristics enter the SME equations with magnitudes an order of magnitude larger than they enter the large-firm equations, and a Wald χ² Chow test rejects pooling decisively at every conventional level (manager block: χ²(8) = 164.7, p ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻³¹; full coefficient vector: χ²(18) = 350.8, p ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻⁶³). Our theoretical contribution is the explicit reframing of SME credit as a person-priced signature contract identifiable in cross-sectional data through the differential significance of owner-level variables. Our empirical contribution is the first joint quantification, on a single representative middle-income dataset, of the manager-priced regime across five outcomes-including a maturitysubstitution mechanism that links pledged fixed assets to lower default risk via the lengthening of debt maturity. The policy implication is direct: state-owned development banks and credit-guarantee programmes-FOGAPE in Chile, the Credit Guarantee Corporation in Malaysia, CGTMSE in India, KUR in Indonesia, the Chinese provincial guarantee networksshould condition eligibility on owner-level information rather than on firm-size thresholds alone.

title: Guardians of the Public Trust: Mechanisms for Administrative Accountability and Ethical Governance

detail.title: Guardians of the Public Trust: Mechanisms for Administrative Accountability and Ethical Governance
detail.abstract: The systematic literature review examined existing research to study how administrative accountability and ethical governance operated through their respective mechanisms. The review addressed the general problem of declining public trust, driven by corruption and misconduct, which imposed high social and economic costs globally. The review followed PRISMA guidelines to evaluate 78 peer-reviewed articles that were published between 2018 and 2023 to identify three research questions that explored factors that enabled or obstructed effective whistleblowing and design elements that determined ombudsman effectiveness and the relationship between these mechanisms and wider integrity systems. The research results demonstrated that whistleblowing achieves success through three required elements which include a strong legal-institutional system and an organization that supports whistleblowers and a specialized method to tackle the psychological challenges whistleblowers experience. Ombudsman institutions achieve their goals through their ability to operate independently from their official powers which include complete investigative authority and their need to gain public support. The synthesis demonstrated that these mechanisms achieve their best results when they operate inside an entire integrity system that depends on particular contextual elements. The three different types of organizations which include internal reporting and external oversight together with supreme audit institutions and anti-corruption agencies need to establish purposeful connections while using technological tools with careful consideration. The review showed that public trust requires continuous funding for both institutional systems and foundational integrity values. The study recommended legal changes that will enhance whistleblower protection rights and maintain institutional independence and establish shared accountability systems for public organizations.

title: Nature Credits as Co-Allocation and Co-Financing Instruments in Environmental Policy and Nature Positive Business and Finance

detail.title: Nature Credits as Co-Allocation and Co-Financing Instruments in Environmental Policy and Nature Positive Business and Finance

detail.abstract: Nature credits are increasingly promoted to mobilize private finance for biodiversity, yet their role remains underdeveloped. This perspective reframes them as embedded instruments within environmental policy, business strategy, and sustainable finance, rather than standalone conservation tools. It argues that nature credits function as co-allocation and co-financing instruments, enabling capital distribution across non-substitutable ecological, climate, and socioeconomic objectives while supporting stacked revenue streams. Drawing on emerging markets and policy schemes, it shows that outcomes are shaped by institutional design, ecological constraints, and actor-specific behavior, limiting the effectiveness of price signals. By identifying differences in financing logics across public and private domains, it calls for adjustments to institutional design and evaluation criteria to ensure that nature credit markets are assessed and governed in line with their underlying conditions and constraints.

title: Mapping the Landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) Adoption in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Cross-Database Bibliometric Study
affiliations: University of Cape Coast and Cape Coast Technical University

detail.title: Mapping the Landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) Adoption in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Cross-Database Bibliometric Study

declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no specific grants from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is currently experiencing a technological compression in the domain of Large Language Models (LLMs), characterised by a hyper-accelerated scholarly response that masks deep structural fragilities. While the region is a prolific documenter of the socio-institutional impacts of generative AI, its visibility in the underlying computational engineering remains marginal, creating a dependency paradox. This study provides the first comprehensive macro-level diagnostic of the SSA LLM research landscape through a systematic cross-database bibliometric analysis. Utilising a PRISMA-compliant dataset of 255 high-quality documents retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and OpenAlex (2017-2026), the study employs science mapping and performance analysis to delineate the field's intellectual architecture. The data indicate a hyper-accelerated annual growth trajectory of 74.04% and a high international co-authorship rate (53.73%), yet expose a profound disciplinary asymmetry. While pedagogical sciences monopolise the intellectual core, technical engineering outputs suffer from near-zero citation impact. While recent cohorts show a natural citation lag, the data suggest the field is transitioning from an exploratory phase toward a descriptive plateau, necessitating a pivot toward indigenous technical engineering to sustain long-term impact. The study introduces the concept of reverse maturation to explain this reactive, event-driven evolution, arguing that the regional research agenda risks permanent theoretical marginalisation within the global knowledge economy. These results serve as critical evidence-based diagnostics for policymakers, highlighting the urgent necessity to pivot from reactive technology adoption toward indigenous computational architecture and sovereign innovation.

title: The Labor of being: Intersectional Social Reproduction through Queer, Intersex, and Neurodivergent Embodiment

detail.title: The Labor of being: Intersectional Social Reproduction through Queer, Intersex, and Neurodivergent Embodiment
detail.abstract: This article investigates the intersections of Social Reproduction Theory (SRT) with the lived experiences of individuals who identify as queer, intersex, and neurodivergent (specifically those possessing the dual neurotype of Autism and ADHD, colloquially referred to as AuDHD). Traditionally, SRT has focused on the domestic and community-based labor required to sustain life and reproduce the labor force within capitalist systems. This analysis seeks to expand that definition to include the biopolitical and cognitive labor inherent in maintaining non-normative bodies and minds. By synthesizing Crip Theory, Queer Futurity, and Intersex Studies, the author argues that the survival and "maintenance" of the multiply marginalized subject constitutes a radical challenge to capitalist temporalities and reproductive norms. The article emphasizes a non-pathologizing approach, defining the "burden" of care not as a product of individual deficit, but as a systemic failure of capitalist infrastructure to accommodate human biological and neurological diversity.

title: Critical Minerals and Materials Geoeconomics: Lessons and Ideas from Past Wars and Strategic Competitions
affiliations: and Fellow in Energy, Minerals, and Materials

detail.title: Critical Minerals and Materials Geoeconomics: Lessons and Ideas from Past Wars and Strategic Competitions
detail.abstract: This working paper examines critical minerals and materials geoeconomics, drawing lessons from past conflicts to address contemporary US strategic vulnerabilities. Facing industrially capable adversaries like China and Russia, the United States must secure global supply chains for modern military hardware requiring titanium, rare earths, and advanced electronics. This report outlines a ten-part geoeconomic toolkit to counter China’s processing dominance and aggressive market manipulation. Key strategies include strategic stockpiling, public-private production partnerships, brownfield processing, recycling, and advanced materials development like carbon nanotube fibers. Ultimately, these insights help American policymakers project economic statecraft to build a highly resilient, expanded domestic industrial base.

title: Gender Roles in Somaliland: A Narrative Review of Traditions, Transitions, and Transformations

detail.title: Gender Roles in Somaliland: A Narrative Review of Traditions, Transitions, and Transformations
detail.abstract: This narrative review synthesized multidisciplinary research on gender roles in Somaliland (1991-2023), employing systematic qualitative methods aligned with RAMESES guidelines. Data were drawn from academic literature, rigorously screened gray literature (NGO/UN/government documents), and 12 ethnographic studies, analyzed through critical discourse analysis. Historically, gender norms were shaped by patrilineal clan structures, customary law (xeer), and Islamic principles, assigning men dominant political/economic roles and women domestic/caregiving duties. Post-conflict transformations-including rising female-headed households-catalyzed significant shifts: Female primary school enrollment surged from 22% (2000) to 67% (2023), urban women dominated cross-border trade (bacdo) and founded 14% of startups, and activism secured a 10% quota for women in local councils (2021). Women's Peace Committees (WPCs) achieved a 79% land dispute resolution rate using hybrid xeer-international frameworks. Despite progress, entrenched contradictions persisted. Customary and religious systems perpetuated inequalities: women received half-inheritance shares or were excluded from land ownership (only 2% of titles included female co-owners), FGM/C prevalence remained at 98%, and clan mediation (maslaxa) often prioritized reconciliation over GBV justice. Educated women faced stigmatization as "qaaxaysi" (rebellious) and reported higher divorce rates when challenging spousal authority. Cultural resistance, framed as a defense of "Somalinimo" (Somali identity) and conservative Islam, impeded legal reforms and political inclusion, evidenced by parliament's rejection of a 20% parliamentary quota in 2024. The study concluded that while education, urbanization, and activism drove incremental change, transformative gender equity required addressing structural barriers through culturally nuanced approaches that reconciled statutory reforms with Somaliland's socio-legal hybridity.

title: The Behavioural Vacuum: Tax Regime Choice, Mental Accounting, and the Awareness-action Gap in Indian Households.

detail.title: The Behavioural Vacuum: Tax Regime Choice, Mental Accounting, and the Awareness-action Gap in Indian Households.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this study. No conflicts of interest exist.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved an anonymous online survey of 155 voluntary adult respondents. Informed consent was obtained electronically prior to participation. No personally identifiable information (PII) was collected, and respondents could withdraw at any time. The research was conducted in accordance with the academic ethics guidelines of Symbiosis College of Arts and Commerce, Pune, under the supervision of Dr. Sarika Wagh.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted as part of the author's M.Com (Finance) dissertation at Symbiosis College of Arts and Commerce, Pune.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how macroeconomic fiscal policy and behavioural finance intersect, with particular attention to the effect of India’s default New Tax Regime (NTR) on the investment preferences of Generation Z and young millennials. Traditionally, the Indian government used libertarian paternalism—framing a portion of the tax deduction through Section 80C—to channel individuals towards secure, long-term savings. Removing this choice architecture under the NTR has left what the study terms a “Behavioural Vacuum.” Through a two-phase empirical design and a stratified survey of 155 digitally active urban professionals, the research tests how regime adoption is associated with asset allocation and psychological heuristics.

The data show that safety-net allocations have dropped sharply: only 20.8 percent of NTR adopters invest in traditional instruments (e.g., PPF, LIC), compared with 52.6 percent of Old Tax Regime (OTR) adopters. The analysis also reveals a two-tier structure of behavioural biases. Policy-sensitive biases (Mental Accounting and Herding) are markedly stronger under the NTR, as freed liquidity is mentally reclassified as discretionary income and redirected into speculative assets. Overconfidence and Recency Bias, by contrast, run at similar levels across both regimes, behaving more as generational traits than policy-dependent ones. The research also identifies an “Awareness-Action Gap” (r = 0.089,p = 0.269), higher tax knowledge does not reduce biased decision-making. Financial literacy alone, in other words, cannot replicate the structural discipline that the tax code once imposed, pointing to the need for new, non-tax nudges—such as automatic opt-out retirement enrolments—to reduce systemic risks and narrow the growing protection gap in India.

title: Clearing Short-Horizon Convexity

detail.title: Clearing Short-Horizon Convexity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict

detail.abstract: Using daily participant-position data from the National Stock Exchange of India, I show that domestic-foreign participant imbalances price short-dated index-option convexity. The regulatory data separate non-institutional client accounts, proprietary desks, domestic institutions, and foreign institutions across options and index futures. When the large non-institutional client side rises relative to foreign institutions, weekly straddle sellers earn about one-third of a standard deviation higher returns and roughly two-thirds of a percentage point higher implied-minus-realized premia. The slope is steeper when foreign institutions account for more index-futures open interest and flatter when proprietary desks are more active. I use a 2024 contract-menu rule that shifts weekly trading across products to show that the pricing relation strengthens where trading is redirected, especially on high-foreign-presence days. Short-dated option premia price where the participant-position imbalance clears.

title:
An Econometric Analysis of the Mincer Wage Equation;
 The Association of Education and Experience with Wages in India
affiliations: St Stephens College and St Stephens College

detail.title:
An Econometric Analysis of the Mincer Wage Equation;
 The Association of Education and Experience with Wages in India
detail.abstract: This paper empirically examines the association of education and labour market experience with hourly wages in India using the Mincer wage equation. Drawing on data from the India Human Development Survey-II (IHDS-II, 2011-12), a nationally representative household dataset, the study estimates an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) semi-log wage equation on a working sample of 5,000 wage-employed individuals. The model regresses the natural logarithm of hourly wages on years of completed schooling, potential labour market experience and its square, and binary controls for gender and urban location. Results confirm a positive and statistically significant return to each additional year of schooling, consistent with human capital theory (Mincer, 1974; Becker, 1964). The experience-wage profile follows an inverted-U pattern, indicating diminishing marginal returns over the career lifecycle. Significant gender and urban wage premiums are also observed after controlling for human capital variables. These findings have important implications for education policy, labour market equity, and human capital investment in India's diverse and predominantly informal economy.

title: The Four-Day Workweek as a Legally Permissible Public Policy Option Empirical Evidence -Legal Compatibility -Ethical Foundations

detail.abstract:
This policy brief examines the four-day workweek with full pay (32 hours, 100:80:100 model) as a legally permissible, empirically supported and strategically relevant public policy option within an evolving European environment that increasingly moves toward working-time reduction.The paper reviews empirical evidence from international pilot programs and large-scale studies, including findings from the United Kingdom, Iceland and recent research published in Nature Human Behaviour (2025). It further examines the compatibility of reduced working-time models with European and international labour law.

The analysis argues that the four-day workweek should not be approached as an ideological demand, but rather as a serious institutional policy option linked to occupational health, wellbeing, productivity and the future organisation of labour.

title: Coordination Overhead and Governance Readiness in Distributed LLM Multi-Agent Systems: An Empirical Architecture Evaluation

detail.title: Coordination Overhead and Governance Readiness in Distributed LLM Multi-Agent Systems: An Empirical Architecture Evaluation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this manuscript. The author's employer, Clayton Homes, had no involvement in the conception, design, execution, analysis, writing, or submission of this manuscript and is referenced solely for biographical context.
