detail.abstract: This paper reports a controlled empirical evaluation of distributed large language model (LLM) multi-agent architectures on a synthetic, short-horizon benchmark. Existing agent benchmarks demonstrate that LLM agents can collaborate, use tools, and operate in interactive environments, but they often undermeasure the internal coordination work required to achieve final task success. We evaluate six architecture conditions-single-agent baseline, orchestrator-worker, graph workflow, blackboard/shared workspace, debate/critic, and bounded peer-to-peer-across 60 stratified tasks and five repeated runs per task-condition pair, for 1,800 Gemini 2.5 Flash executions at temperature 0.7. The study measures task quality, token-weighted and latency-weighted Coordination Overhead Ratio (COR), Governance Readiness Score (GRS), token cost, latency, acceptance-gate outcomes, and failure patterns. All runs completed without runtime errors or acceptance-gate failures. In this controlled short-horizon benchmark, architecture strongly affected coordination overhead, latency, and token use, while architecture explained only a small share of task-quality variance. Blackboard/shared workspace achieved the highest raw mean quality (0.9030), followed by graph workflow (0.8936), but this raw quality advantage was below the preregistered 0.10 practicaleffect threshold and both architectures incurred substantial coordination overhead. GRS was constant at 1.0 across architectures because the shared trace and policy-boundary contract enforced common governance instrumentation; this is interpreted as evaluation-harness validation rather than architecture-specific governance superiority. The results support a task-dependent architecture-selection thesis for controlled short-horizon tasks: multi-agent collaboration should be justified by measurable quality, validation, reliability, or governance benefits that exceed its coordination, cost, and latency burden. The findings should not be generalized to long-horizon web, software-engineering, or enterprise workflows without replication on task suites designed to require delegation, memory, iterative validation, and stateful tool use.

title: Reformulating The Representative Rational Agent (The rra) who Engages with Investment Choice under Uncertainty
affiliations: FISK University

detail.title: Reformulating The Representative Rational Agent (The rra) who Engages with Investment Choice under Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This study infers the very first parameterization of risk aversion that is robust to the governance of investment choice. Let Θ_{t+1}≡ `the off-equilibrium state', and Θ_{τ+1}^{∗}≡ `the equilibrium state' of the world. Also, let μ denote conditional expected returns and λ the conditional price of risk. The formal theory infers a rra whose choice-theoretic behavior is governed by Θ_{τ+1}^{∗}≻Θ_{t+1} and a satisfaction of the property of `equilibrium over time (the eot)'. Suppose the rra's efforts towards Θ_{τ+1}^{∗} are successful. Relative to the {ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}∈{Θ_{t},Θ_{τ}^{∗}} - the existing assets - the resulting asset, ζ_{τ+1}^{∗}, has characterization as either a `safe innovation', ζ_{τ+1}^{∗} that is parameterized by the trio, μ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗})>μ{ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}, μ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗})↛∞, and λ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗})>λ{ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}, which maintains the eot; or a `disruptive innovation', ζ_{τ+1}^{∗}, that is parameterized by the trio, μ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗})>μ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗}), μ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗})→∞, and λ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗})<λ{ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}, that attenuates the eot. For the ζ_{τ+1}^{∗}, there exists a `procedural mechanism (pm)' which sufficiently restores the eot. If the rra anticipates that the rationality conditions which govern the effort for either the ζ^{∗} or the ζ^{∗} are, in the short-run, out of reach, with (t+1)⊂(τ+1), the rra restricts the self to an asset, ζ_{t+1}∈Θ_{t+1}, satisfying, μ({ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}∘ζ_{t+1})>μ{ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}, μ(ζ_{t+1})→μ{ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}, and λ(ζ_{τ+1}^{∗})>λ(ζ_{t+1})>λ{ζ_{t},ζ_{τ}^{∗}}, a trio that maintain the eot. In aggregate, risk aversion has recharacterization as, "the procedurally specified rational effort which facilitates an awareness of the governing conditions that span risk neutrality, that is, indifference to all feasible states of the world". Nonetheless, the evidence that the rra engages sequentially with risk aversion, risk neutrality, then some conditionally formulated risk seeking behavior shows the rra is not parameterized by any specific risk preference. In aggregate, with rationality having implementation as the formation of ordered preferences, utility is solely ordinal.

title: The Limits of Persuasion: Why an Appeal Cannot Cut India's Crude Bill

detail.title: The Limits of Persuasion: Why an Appeal Cannot Cut India's Crude Bill
detail.abstract: In early May 2026 the Indian Prime Minister publicly urged citizens to shift to work from home (WFH), use public transport, defer foreign travel and curtail discretionary gold purchases, in response to the post-Iran-war Brent crude price spike and an associated US$38 billion erosion of India's foreign exchange reserves. This policy paper quantifies, in a first-order partial-equilibrium framework, the crude-import-bill savings that two real policy levers-a mandated WFH directive for white-collar work, and a pass-through of higher international prices to the retail pump-could deliver in a single fiscal year, individually and in combination. The analysis is run across three Brent scenarios-US$80, US$100, and US$120 per barrel-that bracket recent analyst estimates and the U.S. EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook range. Using publicly available calibration data (PPAC, NASSCOM, RBI) and standard short-run own-price elasticities of-0.20 for petrol and-0.41 for diesel, a credible centre-case WFH directive (15 million workers, three days per week) saves US$3.7-5.6 billion in annual foreign exchange outflow; a 10% retail price hike across petrol and diesel saves US$6.8-10.2 billion; and a sequenced package saves US$10.5-15.8 billion-roughly 28-41% of the US$38 billion post-shock reserve erosion. The price lever dominates WFH at low and moderate ambition because the diesel base is larger and more elastic. The contribution is the first ex-ante, multiscenario crude-bill estimate of these two instruments and a framing of the appealbased approach as a category error in a coordination setting.

title: Cyber Resilience under Sanctions: The Structural Dilemma of Iran's Internet Governance

detail.title: Cyber Resilience under Sanctions: The Structural Dilemma of Iran's Internet Governance
detail.abstract: Cyber resilience, defined as the capacity to maintain continuity of critical digital services under conditions of crisis, attack, or infrastructural disruption, has emerged as a central concept in contemporary internet governance. This paper adopts a comparative analytical approach to examine Iran's position within this framework, arguing that severe centralization of international connectivity architecture, in the absence of effective redundancy and distribution, can structurally conflict with cyber resilience objectives. The paper further analyzes the role of long-term international sanctions as a structural variable, rather than a mere political justification, in shaping Iran's current governance trajectory. Drawing on the experiences of Estonia, Singapore, the UAE, and Turkey, a four-dimensional framework is proposed for balancing national security, political stability, economic connectivity, and cyber resilience. The paper concludes that genuine resilience is achievable without wholesale internet isolation, and that the path forward lies in intelligent distribution, infrastructural redundancy, and trust-based governance.

title: Stock Market Investing guided by Risk Management: A Context-dependent Dynamic Asset Allocation Framework and Four-Year Live Trading Evidence

detail.title: Stock Market Investing guided by Risk Management: A Context-dependent Dynamic Asset Allocation Framework and Four-Year Live Trading Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Stock Market Investing Guided by Risk Management (SMIGRM), a tactical investment framework in which real-time risk quantification-rather than return forecasting or targeting-serves as the primary driver of asset allocation decisions. At its core is the RISP 500 [TM] (Risk Index for the S&P 500), a proprietary composite indicator that synthesizes more than fifteen variables spanning the volatility complex, fixed income markets, macroeconomic leading indicators, and monetary policy expectations into a single daily risk score expressed as a historical percentile rank. When the RISP 500 [TM] percentile rank exceeds a user-defined Risk Percentile Threshold (RPT), portfolios rotate to safer assets; when it falls below, exposure to risk assets is restored or increased. This mechanism-termed Context-Dependent Dynamic Asset Allocation replaces the static allocation paradigm with a probabilistic, risk-state-driven approach grounded in three pillars: Statistical Edge, Asymmetrical Payoff, and the Law of Large Numbers.

title:
Engineering Migration:
How Capital Infrastructure Design Can Reverse Population Decline through Demographic Arbitrage

detail.title:
Engineering Migration:
How Capital Infrastructure Design Can Reverse Population Decline through Demographic Arbitrage

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No affiliations with any organizations.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes that state-level capital infrastructure design is a mechanism for demographic engineering. Forensic analysis of Pennsylvania's innovation funding system-using Federal Audit Clearinghouse single audits and IRS Form 990 Schedule I disbursements-documents that founders receive approximately $0.25 of every state innovation dollar, a Direct Capital Ratio (DCR) that has declined from $0.42 in FY2021 to $0.25 in FY2024. Cross-state correlational regressions (n=10 states) yield a statistically significant negative relationship between DCR and net domestic outmigration among women aged 25-44 (β =-0.213, SE = 0.071, p = 0.009, R² = 0.614). I introduce the concept of demographic arbitrage-the strategic restructuring of capital flows to attract and retain mobile entrepreneurial talent-and propose a 75% DCR mandate as the primary state-level instrument. I additionally identify Allegheny County's proposed 18-week paid parental leave mandate as a complementary local retention mechanism targeting the same demographic cohort. Cross-national regression analysis of OECD data (n=17 countries) documents a significant positive relationship between fully-compensated parental leave duration and 12-month return-to-work rates among women (β = 0.0038, SE = 0.0009, p < 0.001, R² = 0.631). Together, these instruments constitute a two-tier demographic policy stack. Cost-per-job analysis across investment modalities documents a 10-18x efficiency premium for founder-direct capital over traditional corporate subsidy vehicles.

title: Informational Feedback Loop, Monetary Policy Decisions and Asset Prices Dynamics
affiliations: University of St. Gallen (HSG)

detail.title: Informational Feedback Loop, Monetary Policy Decisions and Asset Prices Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper investigates, how the Fed and financial markets interact together. More specifically, it looks at the effect on monetary policy and asset prices dynamics, of an informational feedback loop that arises when the Fed benefits from a private signal about the state of the economy, and also considers information produced by financial markets when taking its federal funds rate decision, but that information is endogenous in market expectations about that same decision-e.g. when it looks at the information conveyed by federal funds futures. Using a rational expectations model with a central bank and strategic traders à la Lee and Kyle (2018), the theoretical model predicts that the surprise generated by monetary policy announcements and the subsequent adjustment in short term yields depend on three things: the precision of the private signals received respectively by (1) the central bank and (2) traders, as well as (3) the central bank's aversion to financial markets volatility. By contrast, long term yield adjustments do not depend on the precision of the signal received by traders or the central bank aversion to financial market volatility. These results are due to the fact that the central bank puts a larger weight on fed funds futures compared to its own signal if traders' signal is more informative or if it is more averse to financial market volatility. This has a significant impact on the surprise and on short term yields adjustments, while long term yields react only to the amount of new information revealed to traders by the announcement-i.e. the private signal of the central bank. Using a topic and tone approach (Hansen and McMahon, 2016) applied to FOMC minutes (to estimate the precision of the Fed's signal) and tweets (precision of traders' signal), the paper is able to provide some (weak) empirical evidence supporting the model's predictions.

title: Machine Learning for Scenario-based Prediction of Grid Emissions from Electric Vehicle Charging across the United States
affiliations: Kennesaw State University, Kennesaw State University, Kennesaw State University, Kennesaw State University and Cornell University - School of Civil and Environmental Engineering

detail.title: Machine Learning for Scenario-based Prediction of Grid Emissions from Electric Vehicle Charging across the United States
detail.abstract: Electric vehicles (EVs) produce significantly fewer emissions compared to traditional vehicles running on fossil fuels. However, the increase in electrical energy consumption of EVs from the power grid, driven by their rising adoption and higher vehicle miles traveled (VMT) due to lower maintenance and travel costs, results in higher greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. This research introduces a machine learning model developed to predict greenhouse gas emissions from power plants at the state level as EV energy consumption from the power grid increases. The proposed model is built on the Meta Prophet platform, which is specifically designed to capture temporal patterns and seasonality. Trained using the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) Cambium database, the proposed model provides accurate and continuous predictions of Carbon Dioxide (CO2), Methane (CH4), and Nitrous Oxide (N2O) emission rates from power plants over the coming months and years under eight distinct pricing, taxation, and development scenarios. To demonstrate its substantial potential, we apply the model to predict the increase in emissions of CO2, CH4, and N2O from power plants in response to the growing energy consumption of EVs in 17 of the Cambium Generation and Emission Assessment (GEA) regions. Model projections through 2050 indicate that greenhouse gas emissions from power plants will decline across all regions as EV electricity demand rises. The most substantial reductions are observed in Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland Interconnection (PJM) East and WestConnect South, where CO₂ and CH₄ emissions drop by more than 95%, reflecting their nuclear-heavy and diversifying portfolios. NorthernGrid East, with its high hydropower share 43.3%, leads in N₂O reduction at 91.99%. Conversely, regions like the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) and the Florida Reliability Coordinating Council (FRCC), where natural gas remains a key power source, show more moderate declines between 70% and 83%. These trends underscore that the environmental benefits of EV adoption are highly contingent on regional grid composition and highlight the continued importance of renewable energy expansion policies for sustaining national emission reductions.

title: The Implementability of Punishment: Cooperation under Protocol Constraints

detail.title: The Implementability of Punishment: Cooperation under Protocol Constraints
detail.abstract: Repeated-game cooperation is usually studied through incentive compatibility: deviations must trigger sufficiently severe continuation punishments. This paper asks whether the punishment protocol itself is implementable. Building on the cross-sectional approach to implementable randomization, I model institutional, legal, and technological limits on sanctions as affine restrictions on history-contingent punishment randomization. Strict punishment protocols are stable, while mixed punishment protocols can fail: at an absorbing punishment state, affine restrictions can break the indifference between payoffdistinguishable sanction modes and force restricted equilibria to lose part of the original punishment support. The main result turns this support loss into a payoff-wedge channel: if losing the relevant support raises a deviator’s continuation value, then there are cooperative payoffs that are supportable with unrestricted punishments but not under the restricted punishment technology. Equivalently, protocol constraints can remove otherwise supportable cooperative payoffs without changing stage payoffs, monitoring, or patience. The economic mechanism is not simply that institutions make punishments milder; they can change the feasible geometry of punishment randomization and thereby select which punishment supports can be implemented. The same implementability logic extends to finite punishment phases with history-wise restrictions on punishment randomization.

title: Generative AI and the Collapse of Apprenticeship Labor Markets
affiliations: Apna.Co

detail.title: Generative AI and the Collapse of Apprenticeship Labor Markets
detail.abstract: Human capital accumulates through execution. Generative AI breaks this pipeline. When AI automates the entry-level tasks traditionally used for training and screening, firms face an apprenticeship collapse. Seniors can no longer observe whether juniors are learning or just prompting. We model this as a dynamic moral hazard problem where the immediate productivity gains of AI crowd out long-term human capital formation. The equilibrium is stark: firms substitute away from junior hiring, and the pipeline for future senior talent narrows. The market solves this through expensive, verifiable signals of competence, permanently raising the barrier to entry.

detail.title: Beyond Model Readiness: Institutional Readiness for AI Deployment in Public Systems

publicationDetails.detailsText: 2nd Workshop on Technical AI Governance Research (TAIGR) at ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea

detail.abstract: Many public-sector artificial intelligence systems fail not at the point of model development, but at the point of deployment. Systems that perform well in internal testing may still stall because the receiving institution lacks the approvals, data arrangements, human oversight, operational capacity, fiscal continuity, or legal clarity needed for broader rollout. Existing responsible AI and model evaluation frameworks are valuable, but they primarily assess models, datasets, and developer-side processes, not the readiness of the institution that must use the system in practice. We introduce Institutional Alignment Readiness (IAR), a five-dimensional framework for assessing deployment readiness in public systems. The framework is designed for resource-constrained settings, where gaps between technical viability and responsible deployment are most acute. It is grounded in two anonymized operational cases from a large public education system: an imagebased anthropometric screening tool and a speechanalysis system for early learning risk identification. Both reached technically viable stages but could not advance to broader rollout for institutional rather than technical reasons. We use these cases to motivate a practical readiness framework covering institutional and operational compatibility, data ecosystem maturity, human oversight capacity, fiscal sustainability, and regulatory alignment readiness. IAR is designed to complement, not replace, established AI evaluation tools. It assesses the receiving institution rather than the artifact alone and supports staging decisions such as no-go, pilot-only, or readiness for broader deployment.

title: Generative AI and the Return of the Generalist Worker
affiliations: Apna.Co

detail.title: Generative AI and the Return of the Generalist Worker
detail.abstract: Specialization was the hallmark of the industrial and information ages. Generative AI reverses this. By providing on-demand functional execution-coding, drafting, designing-AI fills in the missing skills of generalists. We model how this shift changes the relative returns to human capital. Deep specialists lose their premium as AI commoditizes narrow execution. Generalists-who possess broad domain knowledge and the ability to integrate across functionssee their marginal product soar. The theory explains why the future belongs not to the narrow expert, but to the orchestrator who can direct machine intelligence across multiple domains.

detail.abstract: We present a systematic anomaly detection survey of 520,000 SIMBAD sourcesclassified as ”Unknown” or ”Infrared Source,” using CatWISE2020 four-band photometry andastrometry. An Isolation Forest algorithm trained on four physical features — WISE colourC12, total proper motion, and sky coordinates — identifies 520 extreme outliers (contamination0.1%). The fifty most anomalous candidates separate into two distinct populations: (i) highproper-motion stars (N = 37, median total pm ≈ 200 mas yr-1) with predominantly normalC12 colours, and (ii) extreme infrared-colour sources (N = 8, C12 > 1.5) with little or no propermotion, consistent with dust-obscured galaxies or unresolved infrared populations. Only eightcandidates receive firm anomaly flags (s = -1), dominated by kinematically extreme halo starswith proper motion exceeding 60 mas yr-1. detail.abstract: Brand theory was built for an era in which consumers found brands through search, evaluated them through marketing communications, and chose them through deliberate decision processes. That era is ending. AI assistants-generative chat interfaces, voice agents, and the autonomous systems that act on users' behalf-are becoming the dominant intermediary between consumers and the products, services, and content that satisfy their needs. In this layer, the brand can be omitted from the answer, paraphrased into the synthesis, or substituted at the moment of action without the consumer ever noticing. This article advances brand erasure as a research construct and lays out an agenda for the work that needs to follow. It distinguishes erasure from adjacent constructs (dilution, disintermediation, algorithmic invisibility), argues that customer-based brand equity (Keller, 1993) requires extension into the latent-space substrate of foundation models, and proposes five research questions that map the empirical and theoretical work the field has not yet done. The agenda is written for marketing scholars, but its consequences extend to information retrieval, platform governance, and the regulation of attribution in AI systems.

title: CRSLP:A Virtual-Real-Fusion Benchmark for Cooperative RoadSide LiDAR Placement
affiliations: Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Hefei University of Technology and Toronto Metropolitan University

detail.title: CRSLP:A Virtual-Real-Fusion Benchmark for Cooperative RoadSide LiDAR Placement
detail.abstract: Optimizing the placement of roadside LiDAR (RSL) is essential for cooperative perception (CoP) under cost constraints. Although numerous surrogate metrics (SM) and placement methods have been proposed, no benchmark exists for quantitative comparison of different approaches. To fill this gap, we introduce CRSLP, a large-scale virtual-real-fusion dataset designed for evaluating cooperative roadside LiDAR (CRSL) placement. By integrating real-world point cloud backgrounds with parameterized microscopic traffic simulation, CRSLP covers 13 distinct locations, each with 9 traffic flow conditions and 8 random placement schemes. This setup yields over 900 test instances with continuous per-frame IoU annotations. Using this benchmark, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study that (i) quantifies how environmental and traffic parameters influence CoP performance via SHAP analysis, (ii) assesses the correlation between nine mainstream SM and mean IoU (mIoU) across diverse deployment scales, and (iii) proposes NeRF-PG, a lightweight neural surrogate that learns a conditional probability grid representation and evaluates CRSL placement via KL divergence. The results show that intersection type is the dominant environmental factor affecting CoP performance after controlling for sensor count. Simple geometric and density-based SMs achieve strong correlations with mIoU, but their non-differentiable nature may limit their utility as optimization objectives. The proposed NeRF-PG-based KL metric, which exhibits exponential relationship to mIoU (achieving R^2=0.64 against mIoU while being 3 times faster than recall_rate), offers the greatest benefit among entropy-based surrogates while being differentiable for placement optimization.

title: Addressing the Energy Trilemma: The Role of Entrepreneurship, Regulation, and Climate Finance
affiliations: Australian Catholic University (ACU), Central Bank of Nigeria,  and Department of Economics & Development Studies, Covenant University, Ota, Nigeria.

detail.title: Addressing the Energy Trilemma: The Role of Entrepreneurship, Regulation, and Climate Finance
detail.abstract: Balancing energy security, energy equity, and environmental sustainability has become increasingly challenging as economies pursue low-carbon growth amid climate risk and persistent disparities in access to modern energy. Although entrepreneurship is widely recognized as a driver of innovation, its role in addressing the energy trilemma remains contested. This study examines whether, and under what conditions, entrepreneurship contributes to resolving the energy trilemma, using panel data for 64 countries from 2011 to 2022. Drawing on the World Energy Council's trilemma indices, World Bank entrepreneurship and macroeconomic indicators, and OECD-DAC climate finance data, the analysis employs random-effects models to capture both within-and between-country variation. The results show that entrepreneurial activity is robustly associated with improved energy security and energy equity, alongside more modest gains in environmental sustainability. Innovation capacity strengthens these relationships, while foreign direct investment and climate finance exhibit uneven effects, tending to support system-level and environmental outcomes more than inclusive access. Regulatory quality emerges as a critical enabling condition that significantly amplifies the positive impact of entrepreneurship across the energy trilemma. Overall, the findings provide crosscountry evidence that entrepreneurship functions as both an innovation conduit and a decentralizing force in energy transitions, underscoring the importance of predictable regulation and better-targeted climate finance for access-oriented clean energy solutions.

title: GRF-Net: Plume morphology-informed reanalysis wind correction for satellite greenhouse gas point-source quantification
affiliations: Wuhan University, Wuhan University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Wuhan University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Wuhan University, Wuhan University and Wuhan University

detail.title: GRF-Net: Plume morphology-informed reanalysis wind correction for satellite greenhouse gas point-source quantification

keywords.keywords: Wind correctionPoint-source plumeEmission inversionMachine learningGreenhouse gas

detail.abstract: Accurate satellite quantification of greenhouse gas (GHG) point-source emissions is limited by the mismatch between coarse reanalysis wind and plume-scale effective transport wind. Existing image-based AI methods often predict emissions end-to-end, obscuring whether improvements arise from physically meaningful wind constraints. Here we propose GRF-Net, a physics-guided AI framework that, to our knowledge, is the first to estimate plume-scale wind speed from single-overpass satellite plume morphology. GRF-Net retains reanalysis wind as meteorological priors and learns residual wind corrections from interpretable plume features, including elongation, width, directional consistency, etc., thereby linking improved emissions directly to improved wind estimation. Trained with WRF-LES plumes, GRF-Net reduced MAE and RMSE of uncorrected reanalysis winds by 51.53% and 54.57%, outperforming machine-learning baselines and single-branch neural models. Independent tests with controlled releases, Carbon Mapper plumes and ISD station data confirmed reduced systematic wind-speed bias across scales. Propagating corrected winds into CO2 inversions for GF-5/ZY-1 coal-fired power-plant plumes increased agreement with EPA CEMS inventories from R = 0.37 to 0.68, while 206 Carbon Mapper cases showed reduced emission deviation from 57.9% to 47.1%. These results indicate that GRF-Net offers an interpretable pathway for reducing wind-related uncertainty in satellite GHG point-source quantification.

title: Probing the Energy Trilemma Pillars: Do Innovation Pathways Deliver Cleaner and More Equitable Energy Systems?
affiliations: Australian Catholic University (ACU), Central Bank of Nigeria, University of Tasmania, Tasmanian School of Business and Economics, University of Tasmania, Australia, Department of Economics & Development Studies, Covenant University, Ota, Nigeria. and Yaba College of Technology

detail.title: Probing the Energy Trilemma Pillars: Do Innovation Pathways Deliver Cleaner and More Equitable Energy Systems?
detail.abstract: Balancing reliable energy supply, equitable access, and environmental sustainability is a central challenge of the global energy transition. This study examines how innovation influences the energy trilemma by shaping energy security, energy equity, and environmental sustainability across 115 countries from 2011 to 2023. Using World Energy Council trilemma indicators and the Global Innovation Index, the analysis applies a long-difference regression approach to distinguish the short-run, transitional, and long-run effects of innovation within energy systems. The results show that innovation can generate short-run disruptions, especially for energy security and energy equity, due to adjustment costs, infrastructure upgrades, and the high initial investment required for new technologies. These negative effects weaken over time as innovation accumulates and energy systems mature. The interaction between current innovation shocks and prior innovation stock reveals positive transitional effects, suggesting that the benefits of innovation emerge gradually through learning, diffusion, and system integration. The findings also indicate heterogeneous outcomes across development groups. Advanced economies experience stronger transitional gains in energy security and equity, while emerging and developing economies show stronger long-run environmental improvements, reflecting technological catch-up opportunities. Mechanism analysis further suggests that trade supports the diffusion of cleaner technologies but may initially heighten energy insecurity and inequality through external dependence. Overall, the findings show that innovation alone cannot resolve the energy trilemma. Its effectiveness depends on governance quality, regulatory support, and institutional capacity, highlighting the need to combine technological innovation with inclusive policy frameworks for secure, equitable, and sustainable energy transitions.

title: Forecasting agricultural drought impacts on crop productivity using satellite soil moisture in water-limited environments
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Maryland

detail.title: Forecasting agricultural drought impacts on crop productivity using satellite soil moisture in water-limited environments
detail.abstract: Soil moisture depletion precedes declines in vegetation productivity by days to weeks,creating a natural prediction window for agricultural drought impacts. We test whethersatellite root-zone soil moisture (RZSM) from the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP)Level-4 product can provide skillful sub-seasonal forecasts of crop productivityNear-Infrared Reflectance of Vegetation (NIRV ) anomalies across drought-prone croplandsof Eastern and Southern Africa. We test three input configurations: NIRV -only, NIRVwith concurrent RZSM, and NIRV with explicitly lag-shifted RZSM, to forecast NIRVanomalies at lead times of 8 to 40 days using a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory(ConvLSTM) model chosen for its ability to jointly capture spatial teleconnections andtemporal lag structure that scalar or pixel-wise models cannot resolve. All configurationsoutperform the climatological N IRv and reduce the RMSE by 22–24%. The concurrentRZSM configuration achieves the highest domain-averaged anomaly correlation coefficient(ACC = 0.555), with the soil moisture contribution growing monotonically from negligibleat 8-day leads to +0.049 ACC at 40 days. When we stratify by aridity, the RZSMadvantage concentrates in water-limited croplands, and the ACC improves by up to +0.09at 40 days when sufficient temporal context (80+ days) is provided. In energy-limitedregions, soil moisture adds minimal predictive value. Our case study of the 2024 southernAfrican El Niño drought demonstrates that the RZSM-informed model resolves the spatialpattern of crop failure approximately 32 days in advance, improving spatial correlation by29% over the autoregressive. Our results establish that SMAP root-zone soil moisture is aviable predictor of sub-seasonal agricultural drought impacts in water-limited Africancroplands.

title: Blockchain technology and sustainable profitability in the automotive sector from an Industry 4.0 perspective
affiliations: Australian Catholic University (ACU), National Open University of Nigeria, Caleb University, National Open University of Nigeria, Australian Catholic University (ACU) and Universiti Tenaga Nasional

detail.title: Blockchain technology and sustainable profitability in the automotive sector from an Industry 4.0 perspective
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between Blockchain Technology adoption and sustainable profitability in Nigeria's automotive sector within the context of Industry 4.0. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to management-level personnel in selected automotive firms. A quantitative survey design was employed, and the data were analyzed using SPSS and EViews. The findings reveal a positive but statistically insignificant relationship between Blockchain adoption and sustainable profitability. This suggests that, although Blockchain offers potential benefits for transparency and operational efficiency, its contribution to profitability in the Nigerian automotive sector remains constrained by contextual and implementation-related factors.

title: A Unified Theory of U.S. Regional Convergence and Divergence

detail.title: A Unified Theory of U.S. Regional Convergence and Divergence
detail.abstract: I develop a two-sector model of regional comparative advantage in which the same primitives-Roy-style labor sorting, location-sector agglomeration, iceberg trade costs, and asymmetric migration frictions-generate both the U.S. regional convergence of 1880-1980 and the divergence of 1980-2020. Falling domestic trade costs, paired with an agglomeration response function, deepen comparative-advantage clusters and compress per capita income gaps in the long run, accounting for the convergence phase. Once domestic integration is largely complete, continued declines in international trade costs become the dominant margin: paired with an infrastructure-access function inherited from those same clusters, they generate uneven regional pass-through under Cournot competition and widen within-country wage dispersion in the long run. A four-step mechanism-cluster deepening, migration-induced skill composition, exposure ordering, and Cournot pass-through-links the two eras and reconciles crosscountry convergence in tradable incomes with within-U.S. regional divergence as a joint consequence of a single shock.

title:
Three Views of Resolution in Carbon Markets 
Contractual, Regulatory and Atmospheric Closure
affiliations: Stanford University - Precourt Institute for Energy, Stanford University - Steyer-Taylor Center for Energy Policy and Finance, Stanford Sustainable Finance Initiative and Stanford Law School

detail.title:
Three Views of Resolution in Carbon Markets 
Contractual, Regulatory and Atmospheric Closure
detail.abstract: Carbon markets clear trades, enforce contracts, and satisfy regulatory obligations, yet atmospheric liabilities frequently remain open even where actors proceed in good faith. This article develops a typology of three forms of resolution-contractual, regulatory, and atmospheric-to explain why market execution and legal compliance do not, by themselves, constitute closure of emissions related obligations. These distinctions matter because market instruments are routinely used to support claims of closure-even when transactions resolve only narrower obligations. Contractual resolution settles private obligations between counterparties but leaves atmospheric conditions unchanged. Regulatory resolution extinguishes statutory duties within a jurisdiction but may diverge from global carbon-budget constraints. Atmospheric resolution differs in kind. It refers to instruments that assert closure of atmospheric exposure, linking emissions to a duty tied to measurable atmospheric stock and pairing that duty with a remedy capable of cure, such that breach does not collapse the intelligibility of the underlying claim. When instruments that resolve different liabilities are treated as interchangeable, markets clear on the weakest form of resolution available. Prices then reflect the ease of generating transferable claims rather than the cost of maintaining atmospheric closure, producing structural incompleteness even under rigorous verification and full compliance. The article concludes that atmospheric alignment is not a matter of improved measurement or more conservative baselines, but of remedial architecture. Carbon markets can function without closure; budget-consistent claims arise only where the instruments used to support them resolve the same atmospheric exposure as the emissions to which they refer.

title: Sustainable Tourism and Circular Economy: Navigating the Path Towards Responsible Practices and Environmental Stewardship in Italy

detail.title: Sustainable Tourism and Circular Economy: Navigating the Path Towards Responsible Practices and Environmental Stewardship in Italy
detail.abstract:
This paper explores the intersection of circular economy (CE) practices and the tourism sector, emphasizing the critical role of sustainability in modern tourism. The paper conducts a comprehensive review of the literature examining CE principles within tourism, highlighting key areas such as energy management, food waste, water management, and waste management. The analysis reveals growing attention to the application of renewable energy resources in tourism, as illustrated through various case studies. The paper discusses innovative methods for food waste reduction, the challenges of managing water resources, and strategies for effective waste management. Moreover, it examines tourists’ behaviors towards CE practices and the implications of these behaviors for the tourism industry. The review of local literature, particularly focusing on Italy, provides insights into hotel circular practices, agritourism, and relevant certifications and indicators. Through this paper, the author aims to contribute to the dialogue on tourism sustainability and to present actionable strategies for advancing the sector.

The three main actions on which tourism should concentrate to achieve more sustainable development are resource efficiency, environmental protection, and climate change mitigation linked to the Sustainable Development Goals (UNWTO). The European Commission established the basis for best environmental management practices in the tourism sector in accordance with Article 46 of the Eco-Management and Audit Scheme (EMAS) regulation. Furthermore, through the “Guide on EU funding for the tourism sector 2014–2020,” the European Union states that effective governance, policies, frameworks, and tools need to be implemented to properly guide and support, also from an economic perspective, the development and promotion of sustainable tourism practices.

In this regard, one of the first initiatives undertaken by the European Community was the introduction of the EU Ecolabel for tourist accommodation services, created to improve the environmental performance of hotels, campsites, hostels, agritourism facilities, holiday homes, and bed & breakfasts by providing efficient guidelines on actions to be implemented in order to reduce their environmental impact. This initiative still remains one of the most widely adopted sustainability measures within the tourism sector.

title: Macroeconomic Drivers of Housing Supply in Kenya
affiliations: University of Eldoret

detail.title: Macroeconomic Drivers of Housing Supply in Kenya
detail.abstract: The imbalance between housing demand and supply has prompted an investigation into the role of the macroeconomic factors on housing delivery in Kenya. Although the effects of macroeconomic conditions have been acknowledged, there is a need to analyse the short-run and long-run effects of these factors to precisely understand the behaviour of the housing market, thereby shielding developers from economic losses. The macroeconomic conditions are operationalized using the inflation rate, interest rate, economic growth, housing price and government expenditure. This study employed a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) on annual data from 1980 to 2024 of the selected macroeconomic variables, sourced from the National Housing Corporation, Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development and Kenya National Bureau of Statistics and the World Bank. The results showed a clear positive effect of house prices and economic growth on housing supply. On the other hand, the study identified a negative effect of the interest rate, inflation rate, and government spending on long-term housing provision. The interest rate negatively impacted housing supply in the short term. The study demonstrated that only the interest rate affected housing supply in both the short and long run. Increased borrowing costs discourage investment in housing construction in the short term and over time. To manage housing policies effectively, it's essential to keep an eye on macroeconomic factors like interest rates, inflation rates, economic growth, and house prices. Staying informed helps predict market trends and match housing supply with demand.

title: Three-Field Neural Operator Surrogates for Coupled Fast-Reactor Multi-Physics Simulation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Three-Field Neural Operator Surrogates for Coupled Fast-Reactor Multi-Physics Simulation
detail.abstract: Self-consistent multi-physics simulation of Generation IV fast reactors---coupling the neutron flux, temperature, and stress fields---requires minutes to hours of Picard-iterated solver time per configuration, prohibiting design exploration and uncertainty quantification. We present the first three-field coupled neural operator that simultaneously predicts T(r,z), φ(r,z), and σ_θ(r,z) directly from seven operating and geometric parameters. Four architectures are compared at matched parameter count (~785k): JointDeepONet, SeparateDeepONet, MIONet, and Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), trained on a 5000-sample lead-cooled fast reactor (LFR) dataset and evaluated on a 500-sample sodium-cooled fast reactor (SFR) dataset generated by a fully coupled OpenMC + OpenFOAM + Code_Aster pipeline. On LFR, FNO with uncertainty-weighted training achieves relative L2 errors of 1.19 ± 0.04% (T), 0.80 ± 0.05% (φ), and 0.84 ± 0.05% (σ_θ) over n=3 seeds---a 56--94% reduction over DeepONet variants---with a 1.04 × 10^5 inference speedup. Controlled ablation reveals strongly asymmetric coupling: T and φ form a bidirectional synergistic pair while σ_θ is a downstream consequence. On SFR, only FNO learns the neutron flux (1.59%); all DeepONet variants collapse to a near-constant per-sample prediction (~89% error), exposing a representational limit of pointwise branch-trunk architectures. Cross-reactor LFR→SFR zero-shot transfer is structurally infeasible; few-shot fine-tuning is task-dependent (T benefits, φ and σ_θ are harmed). These results establish FNO as the default architecture for multi-physics neural operator surrogates on regular grids and define the feasibility boundary for cross-reactor operator transfer.

title: Physics-Informed Transfer Learning for Cross-Scale SOC/SOE Co-Estimation in Battery Energy Storage
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Ningxia University, Ningxia University, Ningxia Normal University, Ningxia University and Ningxia University

detail.title: Physics-Informed Transfer Learning for Cross-Scale SOC/SOE Co-Estimation in Battery Energy Storage
detail.abstract: For megawatt-scale energy storage systems, the joint estimation of State of Charge (SOC) and State of Energy (SOE) is critical for ensuring safe cross-scale system dispatch. However, cross-scale applications—ranging from the micro level of individual cells to the macro level of containers—face significant challenges, including severe distribution shifts, sample scarcity in edge computing environments, and thermodynamic paradoxes inherent in black-box models.This paper proposes a hybrid-driven collaborative estimation framework (TL5-PINN-DPN) that integrates physical priors with transfer learning. The framework first extracts universal features by pre-training a CNN-TCN heterogeneous network on large-scale cell-level data, then establishes a hierarchical dynamic fine-tuning strategy (TL5) to achieve cross-scale feature adaptation under the minimal constraint of requiring only 10% of target-domain samples. To eliminate physical distortions, this study embeds a Dynamic Physical Parameter Network (DPN) at the network’s base layer and enforces an energy-conservation differential decoupling constraint within the loss function manifold.Experimental results demonstrate that the TL5 strategy significantly reduces the time required for cross-scale adaptation to 40.4 s; in a six-month field validation of a 5 MWh energy storage container, the root mean square error (RMSE) for the joint estimation of SOC and SOE was below 1.0%. Compared to purely data-driven models, this framework reduces the peak prediction error under extreme operating conditions from 11.0% to within 4.0%, while eliminating the thermodynamic paradox where energy predictions violate the upper limit of charge conservation. This study provides an efficient and robust algorithmic paradigm for the intelligent and mechanistic operation and maintenance of large-scale energy storage systems.
